[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] SUMMARY Claustrum orchestrates brain functions via its connections with numerous brain regions, but its molecular and cellular organization remains unresolved. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 227,750 macaque claustral cells identified 48 transcriptome-defined cell types, with most glutamatergic neurons similar to deep-layer insular neurons. Comparison of macaque, marmoset,and mouse transcriptomes revealed macaque-specific cell types. Retrograde tracer injections at 67 cortical and 7 subcortical regions defined four distinct distribution zones of retrogradely labeled claustral neurons. Joint analysis of whole-brain connectivity and single-cell spatial transcriptome showed that these four zones containing distinct compositions of glutamatergic (but not GABAergic) cell types preferentially connected to specific brain regions with a strong ipsilateral bias. Several macaque-specific glutamatergic cell types in ventral vs. dorsal claustral zones selectively co-projected to two functionally related areas—entorhinal cortex and hippocampus vs. motor cortex and putamen, respectively. These data provide the basis for elucidating the neuronal organization underlying diverse claustral functions.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Cross-species integration of claustrum snRNA-seq cells Claustrum tissue samples from mouse and marmosets were collected and conducted single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq). The obtained single-nucleus sequencing libraries underwent identical data preprocessing steps as those performed on the macaque samples. Subsequently, we identified 234,986 cells from the mouse claustrum and 109,093 cells from the marmoset claustrum. Clustering and annotation of the single-nucleus sequencing data from mouse and marmosets followed the same procedures as described in above section, utilizing the same marker genes as those used for the macaque claustrum. Specifically, marmoset data were partitioned into 38 clusters, whereas mouse data were divided into 60 clusters. Moreover, using high variable genes identified from the macaque subclass, we annotated subclasses in mice and marmosets, resulting in 16 subclasses for each species.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] After quality control (STAR Methods), the snRNA-seq analysis included 227,750 cells, with an average of 4,664 molecular identifiers (MIDs) per cell and 1,884 detected genes per cell (Figure S1A). Our UMAP analysis identified three major cell classes (‘‘glutamatergic’’ [GLUT]: 122,006 cells; ‘‘GABAergic’’ [GABA]: 34,293 cells; ‘‘non-neuronal’’: 71,451 cells), which were further divided into 16 subclasses (Figure 1B), including 3 glutamatergic (marked by GNB4, RGS6, and ZFPM2), 8 GABAergic (LAMP5, VIP, RELN, PVALB, SST, PDE10A, LHX6, and UNC5B), and 5 non-neuronal subclasses, including astrocytes (SLC1A2), oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs, PCDH15), oligodendrocytes (MOBP), microglia (C1QB), and endothelial cells (FLT1). Most subclasses contained cells from all four monkeys (Figure S1B), confirming data reproducibility, which was further validated by random forest analysis (Figure S1C). The 16 subclasses could be further divided into 48 putative ‘‘cell types’’: 22 glutamatergic, 19 GABAergic, and 7 non-neuronal cell types (Figures 1C and S1D; Table S1). Using ‘‘spatial-ID,’’39 we annotated cells in Stereo-seq maps from two macaques, matching them to the 48 snRNA-seq-defined cell types (STAR Methods). The cell-type distribution was consistent across monkeys (Figure S1E), with the proportions of various cell types similar to those found by snRNA-seq analysis (Figure S1F).

question: What percentage of claustral glutamatergic cells resemble deep-layer insular neurons?
retrieved_docs: [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Co-occurring analysis of transcriptome-based cell types between claustrum and each of three adjacent brain regions, as visualized by the heatmap of pairwise cell-type overlap scores (Figure 2C), indicated that glutamatergic cell types in the claustrum were much more similar to those in the insula than in the amygdala, whereas GABAergic and non-neuronal cells were similar across all four brain regions. Average overlap scores revealed that the similarity between claustrum and three other brain regions varied among different cell subclasses—all insular subclasses but only some amygdala subclasses were similar to those in the claustrum (Figures 2D and S2B). Further comparison of glutamatergic cell types between claustrum and insula was performed by re-annotating claustral cells using insular annotations (Figure 2E). The GLUT/GNB4 subclass was predominantly re-annotated as L5/6 intratelencephalic (IT) Car3 insular cells, with few cells mapped to L2/3 IT cells. Nearly half of GLUT/ RGS6 subclass matched L5 IT and L6 IT insular cells, while nearly all GLUT/ZFPM2 subclass matched L6 corticothalamic (CT) and L6b insular cells. Interestingly, the great majority $( 8 6 . 4 \% )$ of claustral glutamatergic cells resembled deep-layer (L5/6) insular cells, in support of a developmental relationship between the claustrum and insula.38

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Previous identification of claustral cell types was mostly based on cell morphology,67 electrophysiology,68 and axonal projection patterns.9,69 A recent transcriptomic clustering analysis based on single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from 1,112 mouse claustral cells enabled the classification of three types of claustral glutamatergic neurons.35 For a more comprehensive cell typing, we collected a much larger number of cells from the claustrum of macaques, marmosets, and mice. The three previously identified mouse claustral glutamatergic cell types corresponded to the three subclasses of cells that we identified in macaques and mice. Many cell types were further identified in each cell subclass. Interestingly, the great majority of macaque claustral glutamatergic neurons matched well with deep-layer insular cells, supporting the notion that, unlike those in the cerebral cortex, the predominant role of claustral glutamatergic neurons is to support long-range projections to other brain areas.

Unlike in rodents,9,63 inputs from contralateral cortices to the macaque claustrum were consistently weaker than those from corresponding ipsilateral homotopic areas. Strong inputs from the primary visual cortex to the claustrum have been reported in cats73,74 but were not observed in macaques here (see also Jackson et al.8 ). We found that macaque claustrum receives no cerebellar input, whereas mouse cerebellum projects to the contralateral claustrum.9 Together, these findings suggest that there are specific claustral adaptations in different species.

Comparison of singlecell transcriptomic data across macaque, marmoset, and mouse claustra revealed macaque-enriched cell types. Four distinct PSZs were identified in the macaque claustrum that contained neurons projecting to and receiving inputs from distinct sets of cortical and subcortical regions, with a strong ipsilateral bias. Importantly, these zones comprised distinct compositions of claustral transcriptome-defined cell types, and selective sets of macaque-specific glutamatergic cell types in ventral and dorsal claustrum were preferentially connected with cortical and subcortical structures that are related to memory and motor functions, respectively. The organization of claustral connectivity and the spatial distribution of transcriptome-defined glutamatergic neurons that exhibit preferential projections is summarized by the schematic diagram in Figure 7. Our data provide useful information for addressing the relationship between transcriptome-defined cell types and selective cortical/subcortical connectivity that underlie diverse integrative functions of the claustrum in the primate brain.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Notably, we found that none of the macaque/mouse-conserved GLUT/GNB4 cell types exhibited a target preference, while a substantial portion of the macaque-specific GLUT/GNB4 cell types exhibited a projection target preference (Figure 6B, colored in red and blue, respectively). This indicates that a large percentage of the macaque-enriched GNB4 neurons had distinct projection targets in the brain. Interestingly, we identified two macaque-specific GNB4 cell types (GLUT/GNB4/2 and GLUT/GNB4/7) that were enriched in ventral claustrum (containing neurons projecting to the ENTO cortex and hippocampus). Similarly, another two GNB4 cell types (GLUT/GNB4/4 and GLUT/GNB4/5) were enriched in the dorsal claustrum (containing neurons projecting to motor cortex and putamen) (Figures 6B and 7). These results support the notion that transcriptome-defined cell types send projections to and receive inputs from distinct cortical and subcortical regions that are involved in specific brain functions.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Spatial organization of GABAergic neurons Spatial organization of GABAergic neuronsWe next examined the layer and regional specificities of GABAergic cells and found that RELN subclass was predominantly located in L1/2, whereas LAMP5, VIP, and VIP_RELN subclasses were enriched in L2/3/4. PV and SST subclasses were dispersed across L2 to L6, and chandelier subclass (CHC) was enriched in L2 and L4 (Figure 5A). All GABAergic neuron types were distributed across nine cortical lobes with various degrees of specificity: the fraction of each GABAergic subclass was lower in visual cortices (V1–V4); PV subclass was higher in motor cortices (F1–F7) and the entorhinal area; and CHC, RELN, and VIP subclasses were prominent in the prefrontal and cingulate cortices (Figures 5B and S5A–S5C; Table S5). A similar distribution of CHC cells was found in the human cortex.41

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Finally, we characterized the neuronal diversity across telencephalon brain regions, including 6 cortical areas besides insula and diverse telencephalon subcortical regions, including claustrum, amygdala, putamen, caudate nucleus, globus pallidus external division (GPe), globus pallidus internal division (GPi), nucleus accumbens (NA), substantia innominate and basal nucleus of Meynert (SI/NBM), and hippocampus (published data47) (Figures S2E and S2F). In general, claustral cells resembled cortical neurons more closely than they did subcortical neurons (Figure 2G).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Spatial organization of cell types in macaque claustrum The distribution of various cell types in each Stereo-seq section was quantified along both dorsal-ventral and medio-lateral axes (Figure 3D; STAR Methods), and the distribution patterns were characterized as being even distribution, or showing a mediolateral preference, or a dorsal-ventral preference, or both. As summarized in Figure 3E, most glutamatergic cell types were distributed in a non-uniform manner, whereas nearly all (16/17) GABAergic cell types were evenly distributed. For non-neuronal cell types, oligodendrocytes and astrocytes (astrocyte/1) showed preferential distribution, whereas OPCs, microglia, and endothelial cells were all evenly distributed. The consistency of medio-lateral and dorsal-ventral preferences for sections along the rostrocaudal axis is illustrated by four example glutamatergic cell types in Figure 3F. Data from duplicate monkey sections showed similar findings (Figure S4E). Thus, the spatial organization of various glutamatergic cell types is highly structured in the claustrum, implicating distinct input and output connections with different brain regions (see below), whereas the even distribution of GABAergic cell types implicates that interneuron-mediated local circuits are relatively uniform across the claustrum. The observed preferentia localization of oligodendrocytes may possibly reflect the heterogeneity of white matter distribution throughout the claustrum.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] We further constructed a three-level taxonomy tree using the hierarchical clustering of these cell types (Figure 1B; Table S2). Level 1 represents three major cell classes: glutamatergic (969,794), GABAergic (268,097) and non-neuronal (97,298) cells. Level 2 comprised subclasses of these three major classes, each with distinct subclass marker genes (Figures 1B, S1J, and S1K). Based on their gene expression profiles and localization in the stereo-seq map (see section below), glutamatergic neuron subclasses were annotated by their layer preferences (L for layer: L2, L2/3, L2/3/4, L3/4, L3/4/5, L4, L4/5, L4/5/6, L5/6, and L6; see STAR Methods). The glutamatergic neuron subclasses showed substantial correspondence with the projection-property-inferred subclasses identified by the Allen Institute16 (Figure S1L). GABAergic neuron subclasses were annotated by 5 prominent marker genes: lysosome-associated membrane protein 5 (LAMP5), vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), reelin (RELN), parvalbumin (PV), and somatostatin (SST).12,15,16 We noted that the interneuron marker gene calbindin (CALB1) is mainly expressed by SST and LAMP5 subclasses, and the calretinin gene (CALB2) is mainly expressed by VIP and VIP_RELN subclasses (Figure S1K). The 6 non-neuronal subclasses included astrocytes (ASCs), oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), oligodendrocytes (OLGs), microglia (MG), endothelial cells (ECs), and vascular leptomeningeal cells (VLMCs), each annotated by their specific marker genes (Figure S1K).
answer: Long-range projecting GABAergic neurons

In line with previous studies,52–57 we found many claustral marker genes (such as SYNPR, NR4A2, and NTNG2) distinguish claustrum from surrounding structures (Figure 3A). In addition, our genome-wide spatial transcriptomic map revealed that there was a distinct boundary demarcating a region with differential gene expression with respect to the claustrum proper, here defined as ‘‘region bordering ventromedial claustrum’’ (RBC) (Figure 3B). RBC highly expressed CPLX3, CABP7, and SULF1 but not the above-mentioned claustral marker genes (Figures 3A, S4A individual genes, S4B replicate data, and S4C Allen in situ hybridization [ISH] data). The RBC region was most prominent in claustral middle sections. In more rostral sections, a more expanded RBC separated claustrum from dorsal endopiriform nucleus (DEn), which also highly expressed conventional claustral marker genes SYNPY, NR4A2, and NTNG2 (Figure 3A).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] We further identified genes that were highly expressed in claustrum, RBC, and DEn, and compared their expression levels with those in insula, putamen, amygdala, and white matter (‘‘exc’’ and ‘‘ec’’) (Figure 3C; Table S3). The overall RBC gene expression pattern differed markedly from that of claustrum, whereas most genes with high expression in DEn were also highly expressed in claustrum (Figure 3C). We further identified a set of genes that were highly expressed in the claustrum but not in DEn, such as LXN, SMYD1, GAL, and TFAP2D. Although the overall Z score values of TTN and SLC17A8 in DEn were much higher than those in claustrum, further examination revealed that these genes have comparable expression levels in the ventral claustrum (Figure S4D). Notably, many RBC-enriched genes, such as CPLX3, CTGF, SULF1, and NNAT (Figures S4A and S4D), were previously identified as marker genes of cortical L6b or the ‘‘shell’’ region in mouse claustrum.2,35,58 Therefore, we suggest that RBC is analogous to ‘‘claustrum shell’’ or ‘‘subplate’’ in mouse but that it is not a component of the macaque claustrum.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] stantially higher than that found in the three other regions (Figure S7A). Furthermore, the expression level of claustral marker genes in insular L5/6 was in general higher than that in insular L2/3 (Figure S7B), as shown by spatial expression patterns of 6 representative genes in Figure S7C. Thus, the transcriptomic profiles were very different among claustrum, RBC, and insula.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] The macaque claustrum is conspicuously demarcated by the white matter of the external capsule (ec) and the extreme capsule (exc). Single-cell transcriptomic profiles of mouse and human claustrum show that some claustral cells share marker genes with cortical neurons.35,36 However, the overall similarity of cell types between the claustrum and other brain regions in the macaque brain has not been examined. Some macaque studies suggest that claustrum shares the same developmental origin as the subplate (or layer 6b),37 but others suggest that it originates from a distinct lateral pallial region.38 A comprehensive comparison of transcriptome-defined cell types between claustrum and other brain regions could help to resolve these issues.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] SUMMARY Claustrum orchestrates brain functions via its connections with numerous brain regions, but its molecular and cellular organization remains unresolved. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 227,750 macaque claustral cells identified 48 transcriptome-defined cell types, with most glutamatergic neurons similar to deep-layer insular neurons. Comparison of macaque, marmoset,and mouse transcriptomes revealed macaque-specific cell types. Retrograde tracer injections at 67 cortical and 7 subcortical regions defined four distinct distribution zones of retrogradely labeled claustral neurons. Joint analysis of whole-brain connectivity and single-cell spatial transcriptome showed that these four zones containing distinct compositions of glutamatergic (but not GABAergic) cell types preferentially connected to specific brain regions with a strong ipsilateral bias. Several macaque-specific glutamatergic cell types in ventral vs. dorsal claustral zones selectively co-projected to two functionally related areas—entorhinal cortex and hippocampus vs. motor cortex and putamen, respectively. These data provide the basis for elucidating the neuronal organization underlying diverse claustral functions.

question: Injections in which five subcortical structures yielded a significant number of labeled claustral neurons?
retrieved_docs: [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Cortical and subcortical projections to macaque claustrum In order to map inputs from various cortical and subcortical regions to the claustrum, we injected retrograde tracers at five sites (C1–C5) located in different domains of the claustrum (Figure 5A). The tracer uptake zones of C1, C2, C3, and C5 injections were shown to be localized strictly to the claustrum, whereas that of the C4 injection contained some local white matter (Figure S5A). Brain-wide mapping of retrogradely labeled neurons revealed that the five claustral injections resulted in particular patterns of labeled neurons in cortical and subcortical regions.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] We have also injected retrograde tracers at 15 sites in seven subcortical structures and found that injections in thalamus, putamen, caudate nucleus, hippocampus, and amygdala (Figure S4J) yielded a significant number of labeled claustral neurons, which were distributed with distinct injection site-dependent patterns in the claustrum (Figure 4I). Further examination of the percentage of labeled cells in each of four PSZs for each subcortical injection showed that the distribution of subcortical-projecting neurons is related to that of the cortical-projecting neurons. For example, putamen-projecting claustral neurons are located mostly in PSZ4, which contained neurons mainly projecting to motor cortical areas. Hippocampal-projecting neurons were essentially localized in PSZ3, which also harbored ENTO cortical-projecting neurons (Figure 4J). Thus, individual PSZs harbor neurons projecting to selective sets of cortical and subcortical structures with related brain functions, such as motor control and memory processing.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Projections from subcortical structures The five intra-claustrum injections led to labeling in 100 ipsilateral subcortical nuclei, particularly strong in the amygdala and thalamus (Figure 5F; Table S7). The patterns of ipsilateral subcortical nuclei that projected to C1, C2, and C3 injection sites differed in a manner that related to their cortical connectivity. Compared with C1 and C2 injections, the C3 injection labeled more cells in the ipsilateral posterior thalamic nuclei (Figures 5F and S5C), especially pulvinar (Puli, Pull, and Pulm), medial geniculate nucleus (MGmc and MGpc), and lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), which are subcortical structures exhibiting widespread connectivity with visual areas and associative parietal cortex that also projected strongly to the C3 site.

The number of cortical neurons labeled by the C4 injection was relatively small (Figure S5B), and they were almost entirely located in frontal-motor and parietal sensory areas (Figures 5B and 5C). Interestingly, the C4 injection site at the most dorsal extremity of the claustrum is a location that contained cells projecting selectively to motor and somatosensory cortices (Figures 4A and 4D). Likewise, the C5 injection site located at the middle ventral claustrum is a location that contained cells projecting to ventral temporal and prefrontal cortices, including ENTO and POLE (Figures 4A and 4D). Thus, not all claustral injections resulted in dense labeled cells in the ipsilateral prefrontal cortex, in contrast to the recent finding in mouse,9 and different claustral domains contained neurons that receive inputs from and send outputs to distinct combinations of ipsilateral cortical areas.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Interestingly, we found neurons labeled by C1, C2, and C3 injections were rarely distributed in the dorsal caudal claustrum and ventral middle claustrum, neurons labeled by C4 injection rarely located in ventral claustrum, and neurons labeled by C5 injection were absent in dorsal claustrum (Figure 5G). These spatial distribution patterns point to a regional specificity in intra-claustral connections. In addition, by determining the percentage of labeled neurons for each injection site that was located in various cortical PSZs, we found that claustral neurons labeled by C1–C3 injections were largely $( > 8 0 \% )$ located in PSZ1, whereas those labeled by the C4 injection resided essentially $( > 9 9 \% )$ in PSZ4 (Figure 5H). Thus, the intra-claustrum connectivity pattern to some extent reflects the cortical PSZs of claustrum, again implicating distinct functional modules within the macaque claustrum.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] The C5 injection-labeled cells in various ipsilateral subcortical nuclei, including olfactory nucleus and the hippocampus (Figures 5F and S5C). Similar to C2 and C3 injections, the C5 injection also labeled cells in the contralateral amygdala. Notably, as described above, C5 injection site also received projections from temporal cortices, including ENTO, that are involved in memory functions related hippocampus and amygdala. Thus, individual claustral domains receive inputs from selective sets of subcortical structures, which in turn partially reflect their connectivity with the cortex.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Previous identification of claustral cell types was mostly based on cell morphology,67 electrophysiology,68 and axonal projection patterns.9,69 A recent transcriptomic clustering analysis based on single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from 1,112 mouse claustral cells enabled the classification of three types of claustral glutamatergic neurons.35 For a more comprehensive cell typing, we collected a much larger number of cells from the claustrum of macaques, marmosets, and mice. retrieved_docs: [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Cross-species integration of claustrum snRNA-seq cells Claustrum tissue samples from mouse and marmosets were collected and conducted single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq). The obtained single-nucleus sequencing libraries underwent identical data preprocessing steps as those performed on the macaque samples. Subsequently, we identified 234,986 cells from the mouse claustrum and 109,093 cells from the marmoset claustrum. Clustering and annotation of the single-nucleus sequencing data from mouse and marmosets followed the same procedures as described in above section, utilizing the same marker genes as those used for the macaque claustrum. Specifically, marmoset data were partitioned into 38 clusters, whereas mouse data were divided into 60 clusters. Moreover, using high variable genes identified from the macaque subclass, we annotated subclasses in mice and marmosets, resulting in 16 subclasses for each species.

Our UMAP analysis identified three major cell classes (‘‘glutamatergic’’ [GLUT]: 122,006 cells; ‘‘GABAergic’’ [GABA]: 34,293 cells; ‘‘non-neuronal’’: 71,451 cells), which were further divided into 16 subclasses (Figure 1B), including 3 glutamatergic (marked by GNB4, RGS6, and ZFPM2), 8 GABAergic (LAMP5, VIP, RELN, PVALB, SST, PDE10A, LHX6, and UNC5B), and 5 non-neuronal subclasses, including astrocytes (SLC1A2), oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs, PCDH15), oligodendrocytes (MOBP), microglia (C1QB), and endothelial cells (FLT1). [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] SUMMARY Claustrum orchestrates brain functions via its connections with numerous brain regions, but its molecular and cellular organization remains unresolved. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 227,750 macaque claustral cells identified 48 transcriptome-defined cell types, with most glutamatergic neurons similar to deep-layer insular neurons. Comparison of macaque, marmoset,and mouse transcriptomes revealed macaque-specific cell types. Retrograde tracer injections at 67 cortical and 7 subcortical regions defined four distinct distribution zones of retrogradely labeled claustral neurons. Joint analysis of whole-brain connectivity and single-cell spatial transcriptome showed that these four zones containing distinct compositions of glutamatergic (but not GABAergic) cell types preferentially connected to specific brain regions with a strong ipsilateral bias. Several macaque-specific glutamatergic cell types in ventral vs. dorsal claustral zones selectively co-projected to two functionally related areas—entorhinal cortex and hippocampus vs. motor cortex and putamen, respectively. These data provide the basis for elucidating the neuronal organization underlying diverse claustral functions.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Previous studies in rats utilizing retrograde tracer injections in the central claustrum reported labeled cells throughout the entire rostro-caudal axis.63,65 Here we also found extensive rostrocaudally orientated intra-claustrum connectivity. Interestingly, the intra-claustrum connectivity pattern shows subregional preferences that corresponded to the PSZs of the macaque claustrum. For example, tracer injection in PSZ1 rarely labeled neurons in the ventral middle and dorsal caudal claustral regions. Moreover, we found that two macaque-specific GNB4 cell types in the ventral middle claustral region are preferentially connected with the ENTO cortex and hippocampus, and another two in the dorsal caudal claustral region are preferentially connected with the motor cortex and putamen. These observations indicate the presence of well-defined functional modules within the macaque claustrum that are served by distinct transcriptomedefined cell types.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] SUMMARY Claustrum orchestrates brain functions via its connections with numerous brain regions, but its molecular and cellular organization remains unresolved. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 227,750 macaque claustral cells identified 48 transcriptome-defined cell types, with most glutamatergic neurons similar to deep-layer insular neurons. Comparison of macaque, marmoset,and mouse transcriptomes revealed macaque-specific cell types. Retrograde tracer injections at 67 cortical and 7 subcortical regions defined four distinct distribution zones of retrogradely labeled claustral neurons. Joint analysis of whole-brain connectivity and single-cell spatial transcriptome showed that these four zones containing distinct compositions of glutamatergic (but not GABAergic) cell types preferentially connected to specific brain regions with a strong ipsilateral bias. Several macaque-specific glutamatergic cell types in ventral vs. dorsal claustral zones selectively co-projected to two functionally related areas—entorhinal cortex and hippocampus vs. motor cortex and putamen, respectively. These data provide the basis for elucidating the neuronal organization underlying diverse claustral functions.

question: How does the gene expression of the RBC compare to that of the claustrum proper?
retrieved_docs: [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] We further identified genes that were highly expressed in claustrum, RBC, and DEn, and compared their expression levels with those in insula, putamen, amygdala, and white matter (‘‘exc’’ and ‘‘ec’’) (Figure 3C; Table S3). The overall RBC gene expression pattern differed markedly from that of claustrum, whereas most genes with high expression in DEn were also highly expressed in claustrum (Figure 3C). We further identified a set of genes that were highly expressed in the claustrum but not in DEn, such as LXN, SMYD1, GAL, and TFAP2D. Although the overall Z score values of TTN and SLC17A8 in DEn were much higher than those in claustrum, further examination revealed that these genes have comparable expression levels in the ventral claustrum (Figure S4D). Notably, many RBC-enriched genes, such as CPLX3, CTGF, SULF1, and NNAT (Figures S4A and S4D), were previously identified as marker genes of cortical L6b or the ‘‘shell’’ region in mouse claustrum.2,35,58 Therefore, we suggest that RBC is analogous to ‘‘claustrum shell’’ or ‘‘subplate’’ in mouse but that it is not a component of the macaque claustrum.

In more rostral sections, a more expanded RBC separated claustrum from dorsal endopiriform nucleus (DEn), which also highly expressed conventional claustral marker genes SYNPY, NR4A2, and NTNG2 (Figure 3A).

Further examination of the percentage of labeled cells in each of four PSZs for each subcortical injection showed that the distribution of subcortical-projecting neurons is related to that of the cortical-projecting neurons. For example, putamen-projecting claustral neurons are located mostly in PSZ4, which contained neurons mainly projecting to motor cortical areas. Hippocampal-projecting neurons were essentially localized in PSZ3, which also harbored ENTO cortical-projecting neurons (Figure 4J). Thus, individual PSZs harbor neurons projecting to selective sets of cortical and subcortical structures with related brain functions, such as motor control and memory processing.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Delineation of the boundary of macaque claustrum The macaque claustrum is demarcated by the ec and the exc (Figure 2A). In line with previous studies,52–57 we found many claustral marker genes (such as SYNPR, NR4A2, and NTNG2) distinguish claustrum from surrounding structures (Figure 3A). In addition, our genome-wide spatial transcriptomic map revealed that there was a distinct boundary demarcating a region with differential gene expression with respect to the claustrum proper, here defined as ‘‘region bordering ventromedial claustrum’’ (RBC) (Figure 3B). RBC highly expressed CPLX3, CABP7, and SULF1 but not the above-mentioned claustral marker genes (Figures 3A, S4A individual genes, S4B replicate data, and S4C Allen in situ hybridization [ISH] data). The RBC region was most prominent in claustral middle sections. In more rostral sections, a more expanded RBC separated claustrum from dorsal endopiriform nucleus (DEn), which also highly expressed conventional claustral marker genes SYNPY, NR4A2, and NTNG2 (Figure 3A).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] We further identified genes that were highly expressed in claustrum, RBC, and DEn, and compared their expression levels with those in insula, putamen, amygdala, and white matter (‘‘exc’’ and ‘‘ec’’) (Figure 3C; Table S3). The overall RBC gene expression pattern differed markedly from that of claustrum, whereas most genes with high expression in DEn were also highly expressed in claustrum (Figure 3C). We further identified a set of genes that were highly expressed in the claustrum but not in DEn, such as LXN, SMYD1, GAL, and TFAP2D. Although the overall Z score values of TTN and SLC17A8 in DEn were much higher than those in claustrum, further examination revealed that these genes have comparable expression levels in the ventral claustrum (Figure S4D). Notably, many RBC-enriched genes, such as CPLX3, CTGF, SULF1, and NNAT (Figures S4A and S4D), were previously identified as marker genes of cortical L6b or the ‘‘shell’’ region in mouse claustrum.2,35,58 Therefore, we suggest that RBC is analogous to ‘‘claustrum shell’’ or ‘‘subplate’’ in mouse but that it is not a component of the macaque claustrum.

For claustral-cortical projection strength (retrograde tracer injections in cortical areas), the FLN value was defined as the fraction of labeled claustral neurons relative to the total labeled cells across the entire brain (both hemispheres, including cortical areas and subcortical structures). The projection strength of ipsilateral and contralateral claustrum to a specific target area were calculated separately. For cortical and subcortical inputs to claustrum (retrograde tracer injections in the claustrum), we used the extrinsic fraction of labeled neurons (FLNe) to quantify the connection strength. For a specific cortical area or subcortical structure, the FLNe was calculated as the fraction of labeled cells in the specific region relative to the total cells labeled in the entire brain except claustrum. Higher FLN values indicate stronger connection.

retrieved_docs: [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Projections from subcortical structures The five intra-claustrum injections led to labeling in 100 ipsilateral subcortical nuclei, particularly strong in the amygdala and thalamus (Figure 5F; Table S7). The patterns of ipsilateral subcortical nuclei that projected to C1, C2, and C3 injection sites differed in a manner that related to their cortical connectivity. Compared with C1 and C2 injections, the C3 injection labeled more cells in the ipsilateral posterior thalamic nuclei (Figures 5F and S5C), especially pulvinar (Puli, Pull, and Pulm), medial geniculate nucleus (MGmc and MGpc), and lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), which are subcortical structures exhibiting widespread connectivity with visual areas and associative parietal cortex that also projected strongly to the C3 site.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] The C5 injection-labeled cells in various ipsilateral subcortical nuclei, including olfactory nucleus and the hippocampus (Figures 5F and S5C). Similar to C2 and C3 injections, the C5 injection also labeled cells in the contralateral amygdala. Notably, as described above, C5 injection site also received projections from temporal cortices, including ENTO, that are involved in memory functions related hippocampus and amygdala. Further examination of the percentage of labeled cells in each of four PSZs for each subcortical injection showed that the distribution of subcortical-projecting neurons is related to that of the cortical-projecting neurons. For example, putamen-projecting claustral neurons are located mostly in PSZ4, which contained neurons mainly projecting to motor cortical areas. Hippocampal-projecting neurons were essentially localized in PSZ3, which also harbored ENTO cortical-projecting neurons (Figure 4J). Thus, individual PSZs harbor neurons projecting to selective sets of cortical and subcortical structures with related brain functions, such as motor control and memory processing.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Plotting the injection sites that labeled claustral neurons in various PSZs in four different colors (Figure 4A) showed that neurons in PSZ1 projected mainly to prefrontal, associative, and limbic cortices, whereas PSZ2 neurons mainly projected to early visual areas (V1, V2, and V4). The highly localized PSZ3 neurons projected to entorhinal (ENTO), orbital pro-isocortex (OPRO), temporal pole (POLE), and rostral superior temporal polysensory (STPr) areas. PSZ4 neurons mainly projected to frontal motor areas and parietal sensory areas. Notably, neurons in the four PSZs projected to four relatively compact groups of cortical areas that are largely segregated on the isocortex flat map (Figure 4A) and that roughly correspond to different hierarchical levels in the visual systems.60 Hence, PSZ3 and PSZ2 claustral neurons projected to cortical areas of high and low hierarchy levels, respectively (Figure 4F).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Interestingly, we found neurons labeled by C1, C2, and C3 injections were rarely distributed in the dorsal caudal claustrum and ventral middle claustrum, neurons labeled by C4 injection rarely located in ventral claustrum, and neurons labeled by C5 injection were absent in dorsal claustrum (Figure 5G). These spatial distribution patterns point to a regional specificity in intra-claustral connections. In addition, by determining the percentage of labeled neurons for each injection site that was located in various cortical PSZs, we found that claustral neurons labeled by C1–C3 injections were largely $( > 8 0 \% )$ located in PSZ1, whereas those labeled by the C4 injection resided essentially $( > 9 9 \% )$ in PSZ4 (Figure 5H). Thus, the intra-claustrum connectivity pattern to some extent reflects the cortical PSZs of claustrum, again implicating distinct functional modules within the macaque claustrum.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] We performed hierarchical clustering of DZs for all 67 injected cortical areas, with one typical injection selected for each area. This revealed 4 clusters of DZs, reflecting the distributions of claustral neurons that projected to four distinct clusters of cortical areas (Figure 4C; Table S6). The four example distributions of labeled neurons illustrated in Figure 4B corresponded to each of these four clusters. Similar four clusters were also found by a more fine-grained clustering analysis performed on DZs for cells labeled by all 156 cortical injections (Figure S4I). We then pooled all the labeled cells belonging to the same cluster and defined four overall ‘‘projection-selective zones’’ (PSZs, 1–4), illustrated as domains of different colors in Figure 4D. A merged graph of four PSZs revealed that these PSZs were spatially distinct, except that PSZ1 partially overlapped with the other three PSZs (Figure 4E).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] We then compared the cell-type compositions in the DZs for subcortical projections with those in PSZs for cortical projections. We found that the normalized densities of various neuronal types were highly similar for ENTO-projecting (PSZ3) and hippocampal-projecting neurons as well as for motor/somatosensory cortex-projecting (PSZ4) and putamen- projecting neurons (Figure 6C). question: Do macaque/mouse-conserved GLUT/GNB4 cell types exhibit preferential projection targets?
retrieved_docs: [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Notably, we found that none of the macaque/mouse-conserved GLUT/GNB4 cell types exhibited a target preference, while a substantial portion of the macaque-specific GLUT/GNB4 cell types exhibited a projection target preference (Figure 6B, colored in red and blue, respectively). This indicates that a large percentage of the macaque-enriched GNB4 neurons had distinct projection targets in the brain. Interestingly, we identified two macaque-specific GNB4 cell types (GLUT/GNB4/2 and GLUT/GNB4/7) that were enriched in ventral claustrum (containing neurons projecting to the ENTO cortex and hippocampus). Similarly, another two GNB4 cell types (GLUT/GNB4/4 and GLUT/GNB4/5) were enriched in the dorsal claustrum (containing neurons projecting to motor cortex and putamen) (Figures 6B and 7). These results support the notion that transcriptome-defined cell types send projections to and receive inputs from distinct cortical and subcortical regions that are involved in specific brain functions.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] SUMMARY Claustrum orchestrates brain functions via its connections with numerous brain regions, but its molecular and cellular organization remains unresolved. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 227,750 macaque claustral cells identified 48 transcriptome-defined cell types, with most glutamatergic neurons similar to deep-layer insular neurons. Comparison of macaque, marmoset,and mouse transcriptomes revealed macaque-specific cell types. Retrograde tracer injections at 67 cortical and 7 subcortical regions defined four distinct distribution zones of retrogradely labeled claustral neurons. Joint analysis of whole-brain connectivity and single-cell spatial transcriptome showed that these four zones containing distinct compositions of glutamatergic (but not GABAergic) cell types preferentially connected to specific brain regions with a strong ipsilateral bias. Several macaque-specific glutamatergic cell types in ventral vs. dorsal claustral zones selectively co-projected to two functionally related areas—entorhinal cortex and hippocampus vs. motor cortex and putamen, respectively. These data provide the basis for elucidating the neuronal organization underlying diverse claustral functions.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Our cross-species analysis of transcriptome-defined cell types revealed the existence of a macaque-enriched GLUT/GNB4 subclass of glutamatergic neurons. We further examined whether specific cell types within this subclass exhibit preferential projections. We first mapped the distribution of UMAP clusters of the pooled GLUT/GNB4 subclass cells of macaques, marmosets, and mice (Figure 6H). Then, we calculated the overlap score between macaque and mouse GNB4 cell types. Cell types with a maximal overlap score $_ { < 0 . 3 }$ were considered as ‘‘macaque-specific’’ (colored as blue in Figure 6I), while those with a maximal overlap score ${ \geq } 0 . 3$ between macaque and mouse were considered to be ‘‘macaque/mouse-conserved.’’ We also conducted differential gene expression analysis between the macaque-specific and macaque/mouse-conserved GNB4 cell types and found the existence of differentially expressed genes between these two groups (Figure S6J). The spatial distribution of these macaque-specific GNB4 cell types is shown in Figures 3F and S6K.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Matching transcriptome-defined cell types with projection target-selective neurons We further explored the relationship between claustral transcriptome-defined glutamatergic cell types and their projection targets. We first determined the region in the spatial transcriptome map (Figure 6A; STAR Methods) that corresponded to the DZ of claustral projection neurons defined by tracer injection at each of the 156 cortical (Figure 4A), 9 subcortical, and 5 intra-claustrum sites. The density of various claustral glutamatergic cell types within each DZ was calculated, and the normalized density of each cell type across all DZs was then determined. This allowed comparison of density differences of various glutamatergic cell types among the DZs (Figure 6B; STAR Methods). The normalized density of various cell types showed distinct patterns in DZs belonging to four clusters (with the cortical areas listed in the same order as in Figure S4I). For example, the GLUT/RGS6/9 cell type was enriched in DZs of cluster 1 (containing neurons mainly projected to prefrontal, associative, and limbic areas) and in DZs of cluster 2 (projected to visual areas); GLUT/RGS6/ 14, GLUT/GNB4/7, GLUT/ZFPM2/15, GLUT/ZFPM2/21, and GLUT/GNB4/2 cell types were enriched in DZs of cluster 3 (projected to ENTO, OPRO, POLE, and STPr); and GLUT/GNB4/4 and GLUT/GNB4/5 cell types were enriched in DZs of cluster 4 (projected to frontal motor and parietal sensory areas).

Taken together, these results demonstrate that differential sets of transcriptome-defined cell types localized within different claustral zones are associated with distinct target-selective projections to the cortex.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Limitations of the study There are several limitations of this study. First, we identified the macaque claustral cell types based on the clustering analysis of snRNA-seq data and tentatively defined the cell clusters as distinct cell types. This definition of cell types based on transcriptomic profiles could be problematic since the number of cell types classified depends on the resolution of gene expression profiles. Further evidence is required to ensure that the cell-type marker genes represent stable features of various cell types rather than transient cell states.75 Second, we attempted to address the relationship between transcriptome-defined cell types and their input and output connectivity by examining the composition of various cell types within a localized claustral region that sends projections to and receives projections from discrete brain regions. This approach suggests that several distinct macaque-specific glutamatergic cell types are connected to brain regions involved in memory (ENTO cortex and hippocampus) and motor (motor cortex and putamen) functions. A more direct demonstration of selective connectivity of a specific cell type would require cell-type-specific labeling of neurons, together with anterograde and retrograde labeling, which remains to be accomplished in macaques. Third, it remains to be determined whether the connectivity of a cell type with a selective set of cortical and subcortical regions is achieved by distinct subpopulations of neurons within the cell type or by axon collaterals of the same neurons.

[source: Single-neuron_projectomes_of_macaque_prefrontal_cortex_reveal_refined_axon_targeting_and_arborization.md] Comparison of subcortical projections of PT and CT neurons We found that PT neurons in both macaque dlPFC/vlPFC and mouse ORBvl/ORBl projected to a similar set of target areas in the thalamus, pons, and midbrain, including VTA, SN, SC, and PAG (Figure 7H), and that CT neurons in both macaques and mice projected to MD in the thalamus. However, at the single-neuron level, PT and CT macaque neurons projected to significantly fewer target regions than those in mice (Figure 7I). PT neurons in macaque PFC are more biased toward ipsilateral projections vs. contralateral projections than PT neurons in mouse PFC (Figure 7J, left). In particular, almost no macaque CT neurons exhibited contralateral projections, whereas mouse CT neurons showed extensive contralatera targeting (Figure 7J, right). However, by comparing the PT neurons in mouse ORBvl/ORBl with corresponding neurons in macaque dlPFC/vlPFC (Figure S7F), we found a conserved soma location-dependent arbor gradient in SC along the mediolatera axis (Figure 6F). Similarly, the specific projections of CT neurons to MD were also conserved, with a shared soma location-dependent topography along the same mediolateral axis in both species (Figures 6J and S7G). Taken together, in comparison with mouse PFC neurons, macaque PFC PT and CT neurons have substantially reduced the number of targets, while the soma location-dependent topography in their arbor distribution in the subcortical targets was conserved.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Delineation of the boundary of macaque claustrum The macaque claustrum is demarcated by the ec and the exc (Figure 2A). In line with previous studies,52–57 we found many claustral marker genes (such as SYNPR, NR4A2, and NTNG2) distinguish claustrum from surrounding structures (Figure 3A). In addition, our genome-wide spatial transcriptomic map revealed that there was a distinct boundary demarcating a region with differential gene expression with respect to the claustrum proper, here defined as ‘‘region bordering ventromedial claustrum’’ (RBC) (Figure 3B). RBC highly expressed CPLX3, CABP7, and SULF1 but not the above-mentioned claustral marker genes (Figures 3A, S4A individual genes, S4B replicate data, and S4C Allen in situ hybridization [ISH] data). The RBC region was most prominent in claustral middle sections. In more rostral sections, a more expanded RBC separated claustrum from dorsal endopiriform nucleus (DEn), which also highly expressed conventional claustral marker genes SYNPY, NR4A2, and NTNG2 (Figure 3A).

question: To which brain regions do RBC neurons project?

In addition, injections in all cortical areas (spanning over two-thirds of the cortex) led to consistent high claustral connection strength values (Figure S7F). This is sharp contrast to the finding of exponential decrease in connection strength with distance between cortical areas.66 Furthermore, the projection strength from insula was in general lower and more variable than that of claustrum (Figure S7F). We also noted significant differences in the connectivity profiles between posterior and anterior insula, with anterior insular neurons only projecting to a subset of cortical areas (Figure S7F). The projections from insula and claustrum to subcortical structures were very similar, while those from RBC were not (Figures S7D and S7F). Finally, unlike the absence of claustral projection to the contralateral claustrum (Figure S7Ga), we found that both anterior and posterior insular neurons projected strongly to the contralateral insula (Figures S7Gb and S7Gc).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] SUMMARY Claustrum orchestrates brain functions via its connections with numerous brain regions, but its molecular and cellular organization remains unresolved. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 227,750 macaque claustral cells identified 48 transcriptome-defined cell types, with most glutamatergic neurons similar to deep-layer insular neurons. Comparison of macaque, marmoset,and mouse transcriptomes revealed macaque-specific cell types. Retrograde tracer injections at 67 cortical and 7 subcortical regions defined four distinct distribution zones of retrogradely labeled claustral neurons. Joint analysis of whole-brain connectivity and single-cell spatial transcriptome showed that these four zones containing distinct compositions of glutamatergic (but not GABAergic) cell types preferentially connected to specific brain regions with a strong ipsilateral bias. Several macaque-specific glutamatergic cell types in ventral vs. dorsal claustral zones selectively co-projected to two functionally related areas—entorhinal cortex and hippocampus vs. motor cortex and putamen, respectively. These data provide the basis for elucidating the neuronal organization underlying diverse claustral functions.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] After pooling labeled neurons from all five injections, we found that claustrum received strong inputs from essentially all ipsilateral cortical areas except certain regions within the primary visual cortex (V1) and area 1 (Figure 5D), in line with previous findings.2,6,62 Since claustral neurons had a reasonably robust projection to V1 and area 1, the connectivity between macaque claustrum and these two cortical areas is largely unidirectional, supporting the notion of a top-down claustrum influence on V1 and area 1.

question: What are the cortical and subcortical connection preferences of the C3 claustral injection site?
retrieved_docs: [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Rostro-caudal preference of intra-claustrum connectivity Intra-claustrum connectivity plays an important role in information processing,3,63,65 but it has not been explored in primates. Using intra-claustrum injections as described above, we mapped the distribution of retrogradely labeled neurons across all coronal sections of the claustrum (Figure 5G). We found that neurons labeled by C1, C2, and C3 injections had similar distribution patterns along the rostro-caudal axis of the claustrum, with a gradual shift in the dorsal-ventral direction (Figure 5G). Neurons labeled by the C4 and C5 injection also exhibited a pronounced preferential distribution along the rostro-caudal axis. Taken together, these data indicate that there is extensive rostral-to-caudal connectivity within the claustrum, in line with the finding in rats.63

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Cortical and subcortical projections to macaque claustrum In order to map inputs from various cortical and subcortical regions to the claustrum, we injected retrograde tracers at five sites (C1–C5) located in different domains of the claustrum (Figure 5A). The tracer uptake zones of C1, C2, C3, and C5 injections were shown to be localized strictly to the claustrum, whereas that of the C4 injection contained some local white matter (Figure S5A). Brain-wide mapping of retrogradely labeled neurons revealed that the five claustral injections resulted in particular patterns of labeled neurons in cortical and subcortical regions.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] The C5 injection-labeled cells in various ipsilateral subcortical nuclei, including olfactory nucleus and the hippocampus (Figures 5F and S5C). Similar to C2 and C3 injections, the C5 injection also labeled cells in the contralateral amygdala. Notably, as described above, C5 injection site also received projections from temporal cortices, including ENTO, that are involved in memory functions related hippocampus and amygdala. Thus, individual claustral domains receive inputs from selective sets of subcortical structures, which in turn partially reflect their connectivity with the cortex.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Limitations of the study There are several limitations of this study. First, we identified the macaque claustral cell types based on the clustering analysis of snRNA-seq data and tentatively defined the cell clusters as distinct cell types. This definition of cell types based on transcriptomic profiles could be problematic since the number of cell types classified depends on the resolution of gene expression profiles. Further evidence is required to ensure that the cell-type marker genes represent stable features of various cell types rather than transient cell states.75 Second, we attempted to address the relationship between transcriptome-defined cell types and their input and output connectivity by examining the composition of various cell types within a localized claustral region that sends projections to and receives projections from discrete brain regions. This approach suggests that several distinct macaque-specific glutamatergic cell types are connected to brain regions involved in memory (ENTO cortex and hippocampus) and motor (motor cortex and putamen) functions. A more direct demonstration of selective connectivity of a specific cell type would require cell-type-specific labeling of neurons, together with anterograde and retrograde labeling, which remains to be accomplished in macaques. Third, it remains to be determined whether the connectivity of a cell type with a selective set of cortical and subcortical regions is achieved by distinct subpopulations of neurons within the cell type or by axon collaterals of the same neurons.

Interestingly, the intra-claustrum connectivity pattern shows subregional preferences that corresponded to the PSZs of the macaque claustrum. For example, tracer injection in PSZ1 rarely labeled neurons in the ventral middle and dorsal caudal claustral regions. Moreover, we found that two macaque-specific GNB4 cell types in the ventral middle claustral region are preferentially connected with the ENTO cortex and hippocampus, and another two in the dorsal caudal claustral region are preferentially connected with the motor cortex and putamen. These observations indicate the presence of well-defined functional modules within the macaque claustrum that are served by distinct transcriptomedefined cell types.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Mouse claustral neurons projecting to the primary motor cortex (homolog of macaque F1) are mostly localized in the dorsal claustral shell,6,70–72 and those projecting to the lateral ENTO cortex are mostly localized in the ventral claustral shell.35,70 By contrast, we found that F1- and ENTO-projecting neurons are

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Previous identification of claustral cell types was mostly based on cell morphology,67 electrophysiology,68 and axonal projection patterns.9,69 A recent transcriptomic clustering analysis based on single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from 1,112 mouse claustral cells enabled the classification of three types of claustral glutamatergic neurons.35 For a more comprehensive cell typing, we collected a much larger number of cells from the claustrum of macaques, marmosets, and mice. The three previously identified mouse claustral glutamatergic cell types corresponded to the three subclasses of cells that we identified in macaques and mice. Many cell types were further identified in each cell subclass. Interestingly, the great majority of macaque claustral glutamatergic neurons matched well with deep-layer insular cells, supporting the notion that, unlike those in the cerebral cortex, the predominant role of claustral glutamatergic neurons is to support long-range projections to other brain areas.

Spatial gene expression, cell-type distribution, structural delineation, and projection pattern of the macaque claustrum, related to Figures 3 and 4 (A) Spatial patterns of single gene expression in the claustrum, for SYNPR, NR4A2, and NTNG2 genes (coded in red) and for CPLX3, SULF1, and CABP7 genes (colored in green) on one section of the claustrum (EBZ: $+ 1 7 . 4 \ : \mathrm { m m }$ , macaque #1). Scale bar: 2 mm. ven, ventral; lat, lateral.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Limitations of the study There are several limitations of this study. First, we identified the macaque claustral cell types based on the clustering analysis of snRNA-seq data and tentatively defined the cell clusters as distinct cell types. This definition of cell types based on transcriptomic profiles could be problematic since the number of cell types classified depends on the resolution of gene expression profiles. Further evidence is required to ensure that the cell-type marker genes represent stable features of various cell types rather than transient cell states.75 Second, we attempted to address the relationship between transcriptome-defined cell types and their input and output connectivity by examining the composition of various cell types within a localized claustral region that sends projections to and receives projections from discrete brain regions. This approach suggests that several distinct macaque-specific glutamatergic cell types are connected to brain regions involved in memory (ENTO cortex and hippocampus) and motor (motor cortex and putamen) functions. A more direct demonstration of selective connectivity of a specific cell type would require cell-type-specific labeling of neurons, together with anterograde and retrograde labeling, which remains to be accomplished in macaques. Third, it remains to be determined whether the connectivity of a cell type with a selective set of cortical and subcortical regions is achieved by distinct subpopulations of neurons within the cell type or by axon collaterals of the same neurons.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] snRNA-seq library construction and sequencing The DNBelab C Series High-throughput Single-cell System (BGI-research) was employed for the preparation of snRNA-seq libraries. In summary, the single-nucleus suspensions underwent several steps using this system, including droplet encapsulation, emulsion breakage, collection of mRNA-captured beads, reverse transcription, cDNA amplification, and purification to convert them into barcoded snRNA-seq libraries. The generated cDNA was fragmented into short segments of 250-400 bp, and indexed sequencing libraries were then constructed following the provided guidelines. Quality assessment was carried out utilizing the Qubit ssDNA Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100. Subsequently, all libraries underwent sequencing on the DIPSEQ T1 platform (China National GeneBank) using pair-end sequencing. The sequencing data comprised a 30-bp read 1 (comprising a 10-bp cell barcode 1, a 10-bp cell barcode 2, and 10-bp unique molecular identifiers (UMI)), a 100-bp read 2 for gene sequences, and a 10-bp barcode read for sample indexing.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Stereo-seq library preparation and sequencing For each sample, 100 ng $( 2 0 \mu \mathsf { L } )$ of cDNA underwent tagmentation with Tn5 transposases (Vazyme) at $5 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 10 minutes, followed by the interruption of the reaction through the addition of $5 \mu \ L$ of $0 . 0 2 \%$ SDS. Subsequently, a PCR reaction mix $( 7 5 \mu \mathsf { L }$ , comprising Library HIFI Master Mix and Library PCR primer mix) was introduced to each fragmented cDNA sample. The samples were then subjected to amplification in a thermal cycler with the specified protocol: an initial cycle a $9 5 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ for 5 minutes, followed by 13 cycles of a tri-temperature reaction ${ 9 8 ^ { \circ } } \mathrm { C }$ for 20 seconds, $5 8 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ for 20 seconds, and ${ 7 2 ^ { \circ } } \circ _ { \mathsf { C } }$ for 30 seconds), and a final cycle at ${ 7 2 ^ { \circ } } \circ _ { \mathsf { C } }$ for 5 minutes. Following amplification, the PCR products were cleansed using $0 . 6 \times$ and $_ { 0 . 2 \times }$ VAHTSTM DNA Clean Beads (VAZYME, N411-03) before being utilized for DNB (DNA Nano Ball) formation. Finally, the DNBs underwent sequencing on the DNBSEQTM T10 sequencing platform (MGI, Shenzhen, China) with read lengths of 50 bp for read1 and 100 bp for read2.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Brain tissue collection for snRNA-seq Brain tissue collection for snRNA-seqFor monkey #1, the snRNA-seq samples were collected from frozen sections adjacent to those for Stereo-seq. These sections were cut at $5 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ thickness, and 3 to 5 sections for each coronal coordinate were collected for snRNA-seq analysis. Sections were transferred into plastic wells on dry ice and stored in a ${ } ^ { - 8 0 ^ { \circ } C }$ refrigerator. Each section was further segmented into distinct areas on dry ice using tissue punchers $( 5 - 8 \mathsf { m m }$ in diameter). Tissues at the same brain regions (e.g., around the same sulcus) were combined in a prechilled pipe as one sample. For monkey #2, the snRNA-seq samples were dissected from block-face cortical regions of the hemisphere contralateral to that used for Stereo-seq. In the cryostat, the cortical areas were segmented at $1 - 2 { \mathsf { m m } }$ depth using tissue punchers $( 2 . 5 - 4 \mathsf { m m }$ in diameter). After dissection, the samples were immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen and then kept in dry ice or ${ } ^ { - 8 0 } { } ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ refrigerator. Throughout the sampling manipulation, the tissues were carefully transferred to pre-cold tube without thawing.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Tissue-section processing for stereo-seq Tissue-section processing for stereo-seqThe tissue section on the Stereo-seq chip (5 cm x 3 cm or 2 cm x 3 cm) was then incubated at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 5-8 min and subsequently fixed in methanol (Sigma, 34860, precooled for 30 mins at $\scriptstyle - 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ ; 40 ml methanol was added in $1 0 \mathsf { c m }$ dish for each section) and incubated at $\scriptstyle - 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ for 30 minutes. Methanol was then dried out in a hood. Tissue section on the chip was then stained with mixture of nucleic acid reagent (Invitrogen, Q10212) and conA Rhodamine (Vector, RL-1002, working concentration $2 0 0 ~ { \mu \ g / \ m \up| }$ ) for 5 min and subsequently washed with 0.1x SSC buffer (Ambion, AM9770; containing $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { { U } / \mu \mu \mu }$ RNase inhibitor). Section images were captured using Zeiss Axio Scan Z1 microscope (at EGFP wavelength, 10-ms exposure). Tissue sections were then permeated by incubating in $0 . 1 \%$ pepsin (Sigma, P7000) at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 15 minutes (pepsin was prewarmed at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 3 min) in 0.01M HCl buffer (pH 2) and then washed with 0.1xSSC buffer (containing $0 . 0 5 \ : \mathrm { U / \mu l }$ RNase inhibitor) to remove pepsin. In this step, RNAs were released from the permeated tissue and captured by Stereo-seq chip. RNAs were then reverse transcribed for 2 hours at $4 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ .

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] sue and captured by Stereo-seq chip. RNAs were then reverse transcribed for 2 hours at $4 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . After reverse transcription, tissue sections were washed with 0.1x SSC buffer and digested with tissue removal buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, $2 5 \mathsf { m M }$ EDTA, $1 0 0 \ : \mathrm { m M N a C l }$ , $0 . 5 \%$ SDS) at $5 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 30 min, and then the chips were washed twice with 0.1x SSC buffer. The cDNA-containing chips were then subjected to Exonuclease I (NEB, M0293L) treatment for 1 hour at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and were washed once with 0.1x SSC buffer. The cDNAs were amplified with Hot Start DNA Polymerase (QIAGEN). The PCR reaction protocol was: first incubation at $\mathfrak { s } 5 ^ { \circ } \mathfrak { C }$ for 5 min, 15 cycles at ${ \mathfrak { g } } { \mathfrak { z } } ^ { \circ } { \mathsf { C } }$ for 20 s, $5 8 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 20 s, ${ 7 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } }$ for 3 min and a final incubation at ${ 7 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } }$ for 5 min. The PCR products were then purified using $0 . 6 \times$ VAHTSTM DNA Clean Beads and were quantified by Qubit dsDNA HS assay kit (Invitrogen, Q32854).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Stereo-seq data processing Stereo-seq data processingThe fastq files of Stereo-seq were processed according to the previously described workflow.28 The first reads of the Stereo-seq data contained CID (coordinate Identity) sequences, which were aligned to the designed coordinates of the Stereo-seq chip obtained from the first round of sequencing. A maximum of 1 base mismatch was allowed during the alignment process. Reads with MID (molecular Identifiers) containing N bases or more than 2 bases with quality score lower than 10 were removed from the dataset. The CID and MID associated with each read were added to the read header. The retained reads were then aligned to the reference genome using STAR74 and reads with mapping quality score $> 1 0$ were counted and annotated to their corresponding genes. UMIs that have the same CID (coordinate Identity) and gene locus were combined into a single UMI, allowing for 1 mismatch to correct for sequencing and PCR errors. Finally, this information was used to generate a CID-containing expression profile matrix. The entire pipeline SAW can be accessed at https://github.com/STOmics/SAW.

Subsequently, a PCR reaction mix $( 7 5 \mu \mathsf { L }$ , comprising Library HIFI Master Mix and Library PCR primer mix) was introduced to each fragmented cDNA sample. The samples were then subjected to amplification in a thermal cycler with the specified protocol: an initial cycle a $9 5 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ for 5 minutes, followed by 13 cycles of a tri-temperature reaction ${ 9 8 ^ { \circ } } \mathrm { C }$ for 20 seconds, $5 8 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ for 20 seconds, and ${ 7 2 ^ { \circ } } \circ _ { \mathsf { C } }$ for 30 seconds), and a final cycle at ${ 7 2 ^ { \circ } } \circ _ { \mathsf { C } }$ for 5 minutes. Following amplification, the PCR products were cleansed using $0 . 6 \times$ and $_ { 0 . 2 \times }$ VAHTSTM DNA Clean Beads (VAZYME, N411-03) before being utilized for DNB (DNA Nano Ball) formation. Finally, the DNBs underwent sequencing on the DNBSEQTM T10 sequencing platform (MGI, Shenzhen, China) with read lengths of 50 bp for read1 and 100 bp for read2.

In order to map the projection patterns of claustral neurons, we performed injections of fluorescent retrograde tracers at 171 sites distributed across 67 cortical areas and 7 subcortical structures, as well as 5 intra-claustral locations. We performed joint spatial transcriptome and connectivity mapping and uncovered claustral glutamatergic neuronal types that are preferentially connected with functionally related cortical and subcortical structures. Together, these results provide a comprehensive database for studying cellular and molecular organizations underlying various claustral functions in the primate brain. The generated cDNA was fragmented into short segments of 250-400 bp, and indexed sequencing libraries were then constructed following the provided guidelines. Quality assessment was carried out utilizing the Qubit ssDNA Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100. Subsequently, all libraries underwent sequencing on the DIPSEQ T1 platform (China National GeneBank) using pair-end sequencing. The sequencing data comprised a 30-bp read 1 (comprising a 10-bp cell barcode 1, a 10-bp cell barcode 2, and 10-bp unique molecular identifiers (UMI)), a 100-bp read 2 for gene sequences, and a 10-bp barcode read for sample indexing.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Stereo-seq data processing Stereo-seq data processingThe fastq files of Stereo-seq were processed according to the previously described workflow.28 The first reads of the Stereo-seq data contained CID (coordinate Identity) sequences, which were aligned to the designed coordinates of the Stereo-seq chip obtained from the first round of sequencing. A maximum of 1 base mismatch was allowed during the alignment process. Reads with MID (molecular Identifiers) containing N bases or more than 2 bases with quality score lower than 10 were removed from the dataset. The CID and MID associated with each read were added to the read header. The retained reads were then aligned to the reference genome using STAR74 and reads with mapping quality score $> 1 0$ were counted and annotated to their corresponding genes. UMIs that have the same CID (coordinate Identity) and gene locus were combined into a single UMI, allowing for 1 mismatch to correct for sequencing and PCR errors. Finally, this information was used to generate a CID-containing expression profile matrix. The entire pipeline SAW can be accessed at https://github.com/STOmics/SAW.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Tissue-section processing for stereo-seq Tissue-section processing for stereo-seqThe tissue section on the Stereo-seq chip (5 cm x 3 cm or 2 cm x 3 cm) was then incubated at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 5-8 min and subsequently fixed in methanol (Sigma, 34860, precooled for 30 mins at $\scriptstyle - 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ ; 40 ml methanol was added in $1 0 \mathsf { c m }$ dish for each section) and incubated at $\scriptstyle - 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ for 30 minutes. Methanol was then dried out in a hood. Tissue section on the chip was then stained with mixture of nucleic acid reagent (Invitrogen, Q10212) and conA Rhodamine (Vector, RL-1002, working concentration $2 0 0 ~ { \mu \ g / \ m \up| }$ ) for 5 min and subsequently washed with 0.1x SSC buffer (Ambion, AM9770; containing $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { { U } / \mu \mu \mu }$ RNase inhibitor). Section images were captured using Zeiss Axio Scan Z1 microscope (at EGFP wavelength, 10-ms exposure). Tissue sections were then permeated by incubating in $0 . 1 \%$ pepsin (Sigma, P7000) at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 15 minutes (pepsin was prewarmed at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 3 min) in 0.01M HCl buffer (pH 2) and then washed with 0.1xSSC buffer (containing $0 . 0 5 \ : \mathrm { U / \mu l }$ RNase inhibitor) to remove pepsin. In this step, RNAs were released from the permeated tissue and captured by Stereo-seq chip. RNAs were then reverse transcribed for 2 hours at $4 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ .

The sequencing data within the manually annotated cortex region were processed with the Seurat package in R. The cell-by-gene matrix was obtained with the function ‘‘CreateSeuratObject’’ with min.cells $= 3$ and min.features $= 0$ . The percentage of mitochondrial genes (percent.mt) was calculated with the function ‘‘PercentageFeatureSet’’ (using genes ND6, COX3, COX1, ND5, ND4, ND2, ND4L, ATP8, CYTB, COX2, ND3, ATP6 and ND1). [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Stereo-seq data processing Stereo-seq data processingThe fastq files of Stereo-seq were processed according to the previously described workflow.28 The first reads of the Stereo-seq data contained CID (coordinate Identity) sequences, which were aligned to the designed coordinates of the Stereo-seq chip obtained from the first round of sequencing. A maximum of 1 base mismatch was allowed during the alignment process. Reads with MID (molecular Identifiers) containing N bases or more than 2 bases with quality score lower than 10 were removed from the dataset. The CID and MID associated with each read were added to the read header. The retained reads were then aligned to the reference genome using STAR74 and reads with mapping quality score $> 1 0$ were counted and annotated to their corresponding genes. UMIs that have the same CID (coordinate Identity) and gene locus were combined into a single UMI, allowing for 1 mismatch to correct for sequencing and PCR errors. Finally, this information was used to generate a CID-containing expression profile matrix. The entire pipeline SAW can be accessed at https://github.com/STOmics/SAW.

Methanol was then dried out in a hood. Tissue section on the chip was then stained with mixture of nucleic acid reagent (Invitrogen, Q10212) and conA Rhodamine (Vector, RL-1002, working concentration $2 0 0 ~ { \mu \ g / \ m \up| }$ ) for 5 min and subsequently washed with 0.1x SSC buffer (Ambion, AM9770; containing $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { { U } / \mu \mu \mu }$ RNase inhibitor). Section images were captured using Zeiss Axio Scan Z1 microscope (at EGFP wavelength, 10-ms exposure). Tissue sections were then permeated by incubating in $0 . 1 \%$ pepsin (Sigma, P7000) at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 15 minutes (pepsin was prewarmed at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 3 min) in 0.01M HCl buffer (pH 2) and then washed with 0.1xSSC buffer (containing $0 . 0 5 \ : \mathrm { U / \mu l }$ RNase inhibitor) to remove pepsin. In this step, RNAs were released from the permeated tissue and captured by Stereo-seq chip. RNAs were then reverse transcribed for 2 hours at $4 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ .
