[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Stereo-seq data processing Stereo-seq data processingThe fastq files of Stereo-seq were processed according to the previously described workflow.28 The first reads of the Stereo-seq data contained CID (coordinate Identity) sequences, which were aligned to the designed coordinates of the Stereo-seq chip obtained from the first round of sequencing. A maximum of 1 base mismatch was allowed during the alignment process. Reads with MID (molecular Identifiers) containing N bases or more than 2 bases with quality score lower than 10 were removed from the dataset. The CID and MID associated with each read were added to the read header. The retained reads were then aligned to the reference genome using STAR74 and reads with mapping quality score $> 1 0$ were counted and annotated to their corresponding genes. UMIs that have the same CID (coordinate Identity) and gene locus were combined into a single UMI, allowing for 1 mismatch to correct for sequencing and PCR errors. Finally, this information was used to generate a CID-containing expression profile matrix. The entire pipeline SAW can be accessed at https://github.com/STOmics/SAW.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Stereo-seq data preprocessing Stereo-seq data preprocessingThe signal of each gene in all pixels that fell within the segmentation boundaries of the cells was summarized and merged with the location information matrix. The sequencing data within the manually annotated cortex region were processed with the Seurat package in R. The cell-by-gene matrix was obtained with the function ‘‘CreateSeuratObject’’ with min.cells $= 3$ and min.features $= 0$ . The percentage of mitochondrial genes (percent.mt) was calculated with the function ‘‘PercentageFeatureSet’’ (using genes ND6, COX3, COX1, ND5, ND4, ND2, ND4L, ATP8, CYTB, COX2, ND3, ATP6 and ND1). Cells with less than 100 features or percent.mt larger than $1 5 \%$ were discarded. In order to mitigate potential batch effects resulting from variations in single-cell sequencing depth within and across sections of the Stereo-seq map, ‘‘SCTransform’’ with the parameter vars.to.regress $=$ ‘‘percent.mt’’ was used for normalization.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Stereo-seq library preparation and sequencing For each sample, 100 ng $( 2 0 \mu \mathsf { L } )$ of cDNA underwent tagmentation with Tn5 transposases (Vazyme) at $5 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 10 minutes, followed by the interruption of the reaction through the addition of $5 \mu \ L$ of $0 . 0 2 \%$ SDS. Subsequently, a PCR reaction mix $( 7 5 \mu \mathsf { L }$ , comprising Library HIFI Master Mix and Library PCR primer mix) was introduced to each fragmented cDNA sample. The samples were then subjected to amplification in a thermal cycler with the specified protocol: an initial cycle a $9 5 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ for 5 minutes, followed by 13 cycles of a tri-temperature reaction ${ 9 8 ^ { \circ } } \mathrm { C }$ for 20 seconds, $5 8 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ for 20 seconds, and ${ 7 2 ^ { \circ } } \circ _ { \mathsf { C } }$ for 30 seconds), and a final cycle at ${ 7 2 ^ { \circ } } \circ _ { \mathsf { C } }$ for 5 minutes. Following amplification, the PCR products were cleansed using $0 . 6 \times$ and $_ { 0 . 2 \times }$ VAHTSTM DNA Clean Beads (VAZYME, N411-03) before being utilized for DNB (DNA Nano Ball) formation. Finally, the DNBs underwent sequencing on the DNBSEQTM T10 sequencing platform (MGI, Shenzhen, China) with read lengths of 50 bp for read1 and 100 bp for read2.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Tissue-section processing for stereo-seq Tissue-section processing for stereo-seqThe tissue section on the Stereo-seq chip (5 cm x 3 cm or 2 cm x 3 cm) was then incubated at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 5-8 min and subsequently fixed in methanol (Sigma, 34860, precooled for 30 mins at $\scriptstyle - 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ ; 40 ml methanol was added in $1 0 \mathsf { c m }$ dish for each section) and incubated at $\scriptstyle - 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ for 30 minutes. Methanol was then dried out in a hood. Tissue section on the chip was then stained with mixture of nucleic acid reagent (Invitrogen, Q10212) and conA Rhodamine (Vector, RL-1002, working concentration $2 0 0 ~ { \mu \ g / \ m \up| }$ ) for 5 min and subsequently washed with 0.1x SSC buffer (Ambion, AM9770; containing $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { { U } / \mu \mu \mu }$ RNase inhibitor). Section images were captured using Zeiss Axio Scan Z1 microscope (at EGFP wavelength, 10-ms exposure). Tissue sections were then permeated by incubating in $0 . 1 \%$ pepsin (Sigma, P7000) at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 15 minutes (pepsin was prewarmed at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 3 min) in 0.01M HCl buffer (pH 2) and then washed with 0.1xSSC buffer (containing $0 . 0 5 \ : \mathrm { U / \mu l }$ RNase inhibitor) to remove pepsin. In this step, RNAs were released from the permeated tissue and captured by Stereo-seq chip. RNAs were then reverse transcribed for 2 hours at $4 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ .

Each animal underwent definitive procedures for snRNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, or retrogradely tracing without randomization. All experiments were conducted under same conditions, ensuring quantitative results. Details regarding data presentation were provided in the figure legends, while statistical information regarding experiments and analyses was available in both the figure legends and the main text.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] QUANTIFICATIONANDSTATISTICALANALYSIS No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes, but the sample sizes here are similar to those reported in previous publications. No randomization was used during data collection as there was a single experimental condition for all acquired data. Data collection and analyses were not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments as all experiments followed the same experimental condition. Statistical details of experiments and analyses can be found in the figure legends and main text above. All statistical tests were two-sided, and statistical significance was considered when P value $< 0 . 0 5$ . To account for multiple-testing, the $P$ values were adjusted using the bonferroni correction.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Stereo-seq data processing Stereo-seq data processingThe fastq files of Stereo-seq were processed according to the previously described workflow.28 The first reads of the Stereo-seq data contained CID (coordinate Identity) sequences, which were aligned to the designed coordinates of the Stereo-seq chip obtained from the first round of sequencing. A maximum of 1 base mismatch was allowed during the alignment process. Reads with MID (molecular Identifiers) containing N bases or more than 2 bases with quality score lower than 10 were removed from the dataset. The CID and MID associated with each read were added to the read header. The retained reads were then aligned to the reference genome using STAR74 and reads with mapping quality score $> 1 0$ were counted and annotated to their corresponding genes. UMIs that have the same CID (coordinate Identity) and gene locus were combined into a single UMI, allowing for 1 mismatch to correct for sequencing and PCR errors. Finally, this information was used to generate a CID-containing expression profile matrix. The entire pipeline SAW can be accessed at https://github.com/STOmics/SAW.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Stereo-seq data preprocessing The fastq files from Stereo-seq underwent processing following a previously established workflow.43 Initially, the first reads of the Stereo-seq data held CID (coordinate Identity) sequences, which were aligned to the designated coordinates of the Stereo-seq chip obtained from the initial sequencing round. [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Stereo-seq library preparation and sequencing For each sample, 100 ng $( 2 0 \mu \mathsf { L } )$ of cDNA underwent tagmentation with Tn5 transposases (Vazyme) at $5 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 10 minutes, followed by the interruption of the reaction through the addition of $5 \mu \ L$ of $0 . 0 2 \%$ SDS. Subsequently, a PCR reaction mix $( 7 5 \mu \mathsf { L }$ , comprising Library HIFI Master Mix and Library PCR primer mix) was introduced to each fragmented cDNA sample. The samples were then subjected to amplification in a thermal cycler with the specified protocol: an initial cycle a $9 5 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ for 5 minutes, followed by 13 cycles of a tri-temperature reaction ${ 9 8 ^ { \circ } } \mathrm { C }$ for 20 seconds, $5 8 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ for 20 seconds, and ${ 7 2 ^ { \circ } } \circ _ { \mathsf { C } }$ for 30 seconds), and a final cycle at ${ 7 2 ^ { \circ } } \circ _ { \mathsf { C } }$ for 5 minutes. Following amplification, the PCR products were cleansed using $0 . 6 \times$ and $_ { 0 . 2 \times }$ VAHTSTM DNA Clean Beads (VAZYME, N411-03) before being utilized for DNB (DNA Nano Ball) formation. Finally, the DNBs underwent sequencing on the DNBSEQTM T10 sequencing platform (MGI, Shenzhen, China) with read lengths of 50 bp for read1 and 100 bp for read2.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Tissue-section processing for stereo-seq Tissue-section processing for stereo-seqThe tissue section on the Stereo-seq chip (5 cm x 3 cm or 2 cm x 3 cm) was then incubated at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 5-8 min and subsequently fixed in methanol (Sigma, 34860, precooled for 30 mins at $\scriptstyle - 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ ; 40 ml methanol was added in $1 0 \mathsf { c m }$ dish for each section) and incubated at $\scriptstyle - 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ for 30 minutes. Methanol was then dried out in a hood. Tissue section on the chip was then stained with mixture of nucleic acid reagent (Invitrogen, Q10212) and conA Rhodamine (Vector, RL-1002, working concentration $2 0 0 ~ { \mu \ g / \ m \up| }$ ) for 5 min and subsequently washed with 0.1x SSC buffer (Ambion, AM9770; containing $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { { U } / \mu \mu \mu }$ RNase inhibitor). Section images were captured using Zeiss Axio Scan Z1 microscope (at EGFP wavelength, 10-ms exposure). Tissue sections were then permeated by incubating in $0 . 1 \%$ pepsin (Sigma, P7000) at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 15 minutes (pepsin was prewarmed at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 3 min) in 0.01M HCl buffer (pH 2) and then washed with 0.1xSSC buffer (containing $0 . 0 5 \ : \mathrm { U / \mu l }$ RNase inhibitor) to remove pepsin. In this step, RNAs were released from the permeated tissue and captured by Stereo-seq chip. RNAs were then reverse transcribed for 2 hours at $4 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ .

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Stereo-seq data preprocessing Stereo-seq data preprocessingThe signal of each gene in all pixels that fell within the segmentation boundaries of the cells was summarized and merged with the location information matrix. The sequencing data within the manually annotated cortex region were processed with the Seurat package in R. The cell-by-gene matrix was obtained with the function ‘‘CreateSeuratObject’’ with min.cells $= 3$ and min.features $= 0$ . The percentage of mitochondrial genes (percent.mt) was calculated with the function ‘‘PercentageFeatureSet’’ (using genes ND6, COX3, COX1, ND5, ND4, ND2, ND4L, ATP8, CYTB, COX2, ND3, ATP6 and ND1). Cells with less than 100 features or percent.mt larger than $1 5 \%$ were discarded. In order to mitigate potential batch effects resulting from variations in single-cell sequencing depth within and across sections of the Stereo-seq map, ‘‘SCTransform’’ with the parameter vars.to.regress $=$ ‘‘percent.mt’’ was used for normalization.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Stereo-seq data processing Stereo-seq data processingThe fastq files of Stereo-seq were processed according to the previously described workflow.28 The first reads of the Stereo-seq data contained CID (coordinate Identity) sequences, which were aligned to the designed coordinates of the Stereo-seq chip obtained from the first round of sequencing. A maximum of 1 base mismatch was allowed during the alignment process. Reads with MID (molecular Identifiers) containing N bases or more than 2 bases with quality score lower than 10 were removed from the dataset. The CID and MID associated with each read were added to the read header. The retained reads were then aligned to the reference genome using STAR74 and reads with mapping quality score $> 1 0$ were counted and annotated to their corresponding genes. UMIs that have the same CID (coordinate Identity) and gene locus were combined into a single UMI, allowing for 1 mismatch to correct for sequencing and PCR errors. [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Reconstruction of the 3D cell atlas Reconstruction of the 3D cell atlasA total of 119 coronal sections at different coronal coordinates from monkey #1 were used to recover the original shape and topology of a macaque brain. Firstly, we rotated all sections at bin 400 (0.2mm) manually. For the series of sections, a 2D rigid body transformation was computed between adjacent sections. The operation was iterated several times until all sections were aligned to the intermediate sections. Then the sections were assembled to create an initial 3D reconstructed data set, and then the stacked macaque brain volume was aligned to the existing D99 macaque atlas (https://afni.nimh.nih.gov/pub/dist/doc/htmldoc/nonhuman/ macaque_tempatl/atlas_d99v2.html) by an affine transformation. Based on the initial 3D reconstruction, the corresponding sections and MRI images were aligned separately. Finally, all the transformation were applied to the coordinates of single cells at the spatial transcriptome map. A 3D spatial transcriptome atlas at the single-cell resolution of the entire macaque brain were thus created and used to visualize the spatial distribution of various cell types.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Spatial distribution of diverse cell types across the macaque cortex We used stereo-seq to capture mRNAs from all cells of each brain section in close contact with a large silicon chip (up to $5 \mathsf { c m } \times 3 \mathsf { c m }$ ), which comprised regular 2D arrays of DNA nanoballs (DNBs; size, 220 nm; center to center, $5 0 0 \mathsf { n m }$ ). We developed a section-flattening method after cryo-sectioning to obtain even and smooth surface contact between large brain sections and stereo-seq chips (see STAR Methods). Stereo-seq analysis was performed on $1 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ coronal sections from the freshly isolated left hemisphere of three adult male cynomolgus monkeys. In monkey #1, we obtained a total of 119 sections at $5 0 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ spacing covering the entire cortex (Table S3), together with two 10- $\mu \mathsf { m }$ sections adjacent to each stereo-seq section for immunostaining and several adjacent $5 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ thick sections for regional microdissection and snRNA-seq analysis (see above, Figure 1A). For biological replication, we also obtained $1 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ sections from two other monkeys (19 sections from #2 and 23 sections from #3, 3-mm spacing; Table S3). The $1 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ section thickness, together with section preservation procedures that reduced mRNA diffusion, facilitated spatial transcriptome analysis at the single-cell resolution.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] DISCUSSION In this study, we have performed a comprehensive spatial transcriptome analysis of the entire macaque monkey cortex with single-cell resolution, using a recently developed stereo-seq technology. Our brain-wide transcriptome analysis was based on 161 coronal sections across the left hemisphere of three male macaque brains. The reproducibility of our data was confirmed by gene profiles and cell compositions mapped in sections of similar coronal coordinates from three monkeys. Our interactive web portal offers a useful resource for the research community.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Limitations of the study Limitations of the studyThe average number of genes captured per cell $( \sim 5 0 0 )$ by the present method was higher than that found by using previously reported methods,28 although it remained much lower than that obtained by conventional snRNA-seq method. We have partially circumvented the problem by using our snRNA-seq data to assist cell-type identification. Technical improvement in the mRNA-capturing capability and combination with protein recognition may further elevate the sensitivity and precision of the spatial-resolved cell taxonomy in the brain. The 3D spatial transcriptome atlas at the single-cell resolution was based on a total of 119 coronal sections with $5 0 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ spacing profiled in this study covering all macaque cortical regions, which could be extended to whole brain by adding sagittal sections. In addition, only male monkeys were used in this study, and the sexual dimorphism of the gene expression patterns of the macaque brain needs to be examined in the future.

For each coronal section, the cortical region and layer parcellation were manually delineated on Stereo-seq data background, based on cytoarchitectual pattern (eg. cell density, cell size) revealed by total mRNA expression, nucleic acid staining, and NeuN staing of adjacent sections.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Stereo-seq data processing Stereo-seq data processingThe fastq files of Stereo-seq were processed according to the previously described workflow.28 The first reads of the Stereo-seq data contained CID (coordinate Identity) sequences, which were aligned to the designed coordinates of the Stereo-seq chip obtained from the first round of sequencing. A maximum of 1 base mismatch was allowed during the alignment process. Reads with MID (molecular Identifiers) containing N bases or more than 2 bases with quality score lower than 10 were removed from the dataset. The CID and MID associated with each read were added to the read header. The retained reads were then aligned to the reference genome using STAR74 and reads with mapping quality score $> 1 0$ were counted and annotated to their corresponding genes. UMIs that have the same CID (coordinate Identity) and gene locus were combined into a single UMI, allowing for 1 mismatch to correct for sequencing and PCR errors. Finally, this information was used to generate a CID-containing expression profile matrix. The entire pipeline SAW can be accessed at https://github.com/STOmics/SAW.

retrieved_docs: [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] snRNA-seq library construction and sequencing The DNBelab C Series High-throughput Single-cell System (BGI-research) was employed for the preparation of snRNA-seq libraries. In summary, the single-nucleus suspensions underwent several steps using this system, including droplet encapsulation, emulsion breakage, collection of mRNA-captured beads, reverse transcription, cDNA amplification, and purification to convert them into barcoded snRNA-seq libraries. The generated cDNA was fragmented into short segments of 250-400 bp, and indexed sequencing libraries were then constructed following the provided guidelines. Quality assessment was carried out utilizing the Qubit ssDNA Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100. Subsequently, all libraries underwent sequencing on the DIPSEQ T1 platform (China National GeneBank) using pair-end sequencing. The sequencing data comprised a 30-bp read 1 (comprising a 10-bp cell barcode 1, a 10-bp cell barcode 2, and 10-bp unique molecular identifiers (UMI)), a 100-bp read 2 for gene sequences, and a 10-bp barcode read for sample indexing.

question: What is the p-value threshold for determining preferred cell type distribution in the claustrum?
retrieved_docs: [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] To assess whether a cell type exhibited a preference within the claustrum along the medial-lateral (ML) or dorsal-ventral (DV) axis, we conducted KS test comparing the standardized position values of a given cell type against all cells within one section. The p-values obtained from the KS test were first corrected using the Bonferroni method for all cell types within one section. Then, Fisher’s method was applied to integrate the corrected p-values for each cell type across all sections. Only cell types with integrated p-values $\leq 0 . 0 0 1$ in both macaques were considered to have a preferred distribution along the ML or DV axis. Only cell types with in average at least 10 cells in one section were included in this analysis.

For instance, cell samples taken from the overlapping areas of "PSZ1&PSZ2" were randomly divided into two groups: one classified as PSZ1 and the other as PSZ2. After completing the sample allocation, we performed differential gene expression analysis for each cell type using the ‘SeuratWrappers::RunPrestoAll‘ function on the LogNormalized gene expression data. The PSZ region of origin for each cell was used as the grouping factor, with the parameter "only.pos $\mathbf { \mu } = \mathsf { T } ^ { \ " }$ to extract potential upregulated differentially expressed genes. Finally, we filtered the results based on the following thresholds: p_val_ad $< 0 . 0 5$ , auc $> 0 . 5$ , avg_log2FC > 0.5, and pct $> 0 . 2$ , ensuring the significance and reliability of the identified gene expression patterns.

Subsequently, the trained model was applied to all single-nuclei data using the ‘prediction‘ function. The model assesses the probability of the dominant class for each nucleus, assigning each nucleus to the nuclei class with the highest probability. Nuclei with a probability $< 0 . 9$ were discarded. The snRNA-seq datasets from these four regions of macaque #2 and #3 were down-sampled by cluster to ensure consistency in cell numbers across regions, for each claustrum cluster, 300 cells were selected, with all available cells used if the cluster contained fewer than 300. Our UMAP analysis identified three major cell classes (‘‘glutamatergic’’ [GLUT]: 122,006 cells; ‘‘GABAergic’’ [GABA]: 34,293 cells; ‘‘non-neuronal’’: 71,451 cells), which were further divided into 16 subclasses (Figure 1B), including 3 glutamatergic (marked by GNB4, RGS6, and ZFPM2), 8 GABAergic (LAMP5, VIP, RELN, PVALB, SST, PDE10A, LHX6, and UNC5B), and 5 non-neuronal subclasses, including astrocytes (SLC1A2), oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs, PCDH15), oligodendrocytes (MOBP), microglia (C1QB), and endothelial cells (FLT1). Most subclasses contained cells from all four monkeys (Figure S1B), confirming data reproducibility, which was further validated by random forest analysis (Figure S1C). The 16 subclasses could be further divided into 48 putative ‘‘cell types’’: 22 glutamatergic, 19 GABAergic, and 7 non-neuronal cell types (Figures 1C and S1D; Table S1). Using ‘‘spatial-ID,’’39 we annotated cells in Stereo-seq maps from two macaques, matching them to the 48 snRNA-seq-defined cell types (STAR Methods). The cell-type distribution was consistent across monkeys (Figure S1E), with the proportions of various cell types similar to those found by snRNA-seq analysis (Figure S1F).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Cell clustering and cell-type identification using snRNA-seq data Cell clustering and cell-type identification using snRNA-seq dataBasic processing and visualization of the snRNA-seq data were performed with the Scanpy (v.1.9.1) in Python (v.3.8.13). We discarded cells with the number of genes (nFeatureRNA) less than 1000, the molecule to gene ratio (nCount/nFeature) less than 1.2 and the percentage of mitochondrial genes (percent.mt) larger than $5 \%$ . After the first quality control, 1,493,240 cells were remained for the following analyses. The data were log normalized and scaled to 10,000 transcripts per cell. Genes with high variations across cells were identified with the ‘‘sc.pp.highly_variable_genes’’ function with default parameters (top 3000). Next, principal component analysis (PCA) was carried out, and the top 40 principal components (PCs) were used by BBKNN method to remove the batch effect among two macaques. Graph-based clustering (Leiden) was performed with resolution of 1.0 on the graph-representation output of BBKNN. This method resulted in 33 cell clusters. We used uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) method to visualize the distance between cells in 2D space. We then categorized the 33 cell clusters into 3 categories based on classical marker genes, including glutamatergic neurons, GABAergic neurons and non-neuronal cells. Then the three categories of cells were further iteratively classified into more cell clusters with higher resolution.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Image registration and image-based single cell segmentation of Stereo-seq data We performed the same strategies of image registration and cell segmentation as in another work43 for identifying single cells in Stereo-seq data. Initially, we converted the captured mRNAs of each section into a 16-bit image, with the UMI counts of each coordinate as its pixel value. Next, nucleic acid staining images of sections were automatically registered into the corresponding mRNA coordinate spaces, utilizing the periodical track lines pre-engraved in the chip planes. In this step, we first applied adaptive brightness and contract adjustment on the images, enhancing the features and reducing the impact of uneven staining. We then employed 1D Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) operators, used separately in the row and column directions, to detect track lines in both nucleic acid staining and mRNA images and estimate the relative rotation between the two channels. The relative scale and translation were next calculated based on the detected periodical track lines using RANSAC algorithm. The image registration procedure was implemented with Scikit-image package (v.0.19.2) in Python (v.3.9.7).

The trained DNN was used to compute the initial probabilities of defined cell types for each single cell on the Stereo-seq data. Then the spatial neighborhood information of cells on Stereoseq data was encapsulated into an adjacency matrix with normalized Euclidean distances as values for non-zero elements. Next, a graph convolution network (GCN) took the initial probabilities, the distance-weighted adjacency matrix and the original gene expression of cells as inputs to generate the final probabilities of cell types for each cell. The GCN contained two autoencoders, that is, a deep autoencoder for gene expression representations and a variational graph autoencoder for spatial neighborhood information representations, and a classifier block. The two autoencoders were trained by reconstruction losses via a self-supervised learning strategy, forcing the model to focus on the features of Stereo-seq data itself. [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Cell type annotation of single cells in the Stereo-seq map To annotate single cells in the Stereo-seq map, we employed Spatial-ID,39 a robust and effective cell type annotation algorithm. First, we trained a Deep Neural Network (DNN) on the snRNA-seq data with cell types identified in the snRNA-seq clustering analysis. In this phase, the intersecting gene set from both snRNA-seq and Stereo-seq data was used as the model input. The DNN model was trained 30 epochs with learning rate of $3 \mathsf { e } ^ { - 4 }$ and weight decay of $1 { \tt e } ^ { - 6 }$ . Post-training, the model was deployed to predict the initial probabilities of cell types for each single cell in the Stereo-seq map. Next, we utilized a Graph Convolution Network (GCN) to extract the feature represents of gene expressions and spatial neighborhood information, which then generated the final probabilities of cells in Stereo-seq data. The spatial neighborhood information was denoted as an adjacency matrix with normalized Euclidean distances as weights. The GCN model comprised three blocks: a deep autoencoder for distilling gene expression features, a variational graph autoencoder for spatial neighborhood feature extraction, and finally a classifier block for connecting the extracted features with predefined cell types. The GCN model was trained through two reconstruction losses via a self-supervised learning strategy and a classification loss with learning rate of $1 { \tt e } ^ { - 2 }$ and weight_decay of 1e-4 for 200 epochs.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Stereo-seq data processing Stereo-seq data processingThe fastq files of Stereo-seq were processed according to the previously described workflow.28 The first reads of the Stereo-seq data contained CID (coordinate Identity) sequences, which were aligned to the designed coordinates of the Stereo-seq chip obtained from the first round of sequencing. A maximum of 1 base mismatch was allowed during the alignment process. Reads with MID (molecular Identifiers) containing N bases or more than 2 bases with quality score lower than 10 were removed from the dataset. The CID and MID associated with each read were added to the read header. The retained reads were then aligned to the reference genome using STAR74 and reads with mapping quality score $> 1 0$ were counted and annotated to their corresponding genes. UMIs that have the same CID (coordinate Identity) and gene locus were combined into a single UMI, allowing for 1 mismatch to correct for sequencing and PCR errors. Finally, this information was used to generate a CID-containing expression profile matrix. The entire pipeline SAW can be accessed at https://github.com/STOmics/SAW.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] To segment single cells in nucleic acid staining images, we leveraged mask R-CNN-based deep learning models that were trained with annotations from Concanavalin A (ConA) staining images. ConA staining images, which stain the cell membranes, provide distinct boundaries between cells, hence facilitating easier distinction and manual annotation as compared to nucleic acid staining images. For the training set annotation, we used an active learning strategy, keeping human involvement to a minimum. To start, we manually labeled a small number of cells in the ConA images for training a mask R-CNN-based deep learning model, denoted as ConA model. The trained ConA model was applied to predict the cells of unlabeled ConA images. After a manual check and modification, these cell labels were then sent back to update the ConA model. We continued the cyclic process until enough annotations were acquired. The obtained cell annotations of ConA images were transferred to the corresponding nuclei acid staining images as the training set of another mask R-CNN-based deep learning model, denoted as nucleic acid model. Finally, the well-trained nuclei acid model was deployed on nucleic acid staining images to perform single cell segmentation. The cell segmentation procedure was implemented with MMDetection package (v.2.25.1) in Python (v.3.8.13).
answer: Single cells in Stereo-seq images are segmented using mask R-CNN-based deep learning models trained with ConA staining annotations, and cell types are assigned using the Spatial-ID algorithm combined with a Graph Convolution Network (GCN).

question: How are the captured mRNAs converted for image registration, and how are spatial positions normalized for distribution analysis?
retrieved_docs: [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] For registration, we first computed the similarity matrix of the claustrum embeddings between two animals. We then used dynamic time warping (DTW) to find the optimal matching path, avoiding the influence of jitters in slice spacing during experiments. Next, we used the symmetric diffeomorphic registration (SyN) algorithm provided by Dipy to compute the diffeomorphic mapping between corresponding slices. The registration from the connectome to the transcriptome was completed using Thin Plate Splines (TPS) after manual landmark annotation by experts, with the algorithm provided by ITK. This provides the most accurate transformation. The software and versions involved in this process were: Python (v.3.11.3), PyTorch (v.2.0.1), Albumentations (v.1.3.1), and Dipy (v.1.8.0).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Image-based single-cell segmentation of stereo-seq data Image-based single-cell segmentation of stereo-seq dataFor single cell segmentation of the Stereo-seq data, nucleic acid staining images were automatically registered into mRNA coordinate space based on periodical track lines pre-engraved in the chip plane. In this step, the captured mRNAs of a section were treated as an image with the UMI counts at each position as its pixel value. On both nucleic acid staining and mRNA images, we applied 1D Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) operators (sigma = 5e-4) along the row and column directions respectively to detect track lines, following two rules: (1) The track lines are most likely located at where the intensity values change rapidly in the images, which can be identified

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] at the peaks through a LoG filter. (2) The registered track lines should roughly lie along the horizontal or vertical directions. We then obtained the averaged angle between the detected track lines in the nucleic acid staining image and those in the corresponding RNA image as the rotation angle between the two images. Next, we used the averaged interval of the periodical track lines in both nucleic acid staining and mRNA images to compute the relative scale. Finally, we calculated the relative translation using RANSAC algorithm (min_samples $= 3$ , residual_threshold $= 5$ ) with the detected track lines in the mRNA images and the rotated and scaled track lines in the nucleic acid staining images as inputs. With the rotation, scale and translation parameters, nucleic acid staining images can be registered into the coordinate space of mRNA images. The whole registration was implemented with Scikit-image package (v.0.18.3) in Python (v.3.9.7).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Image registration and image-based single cell segmentation of Stereo-seq data We performed the same strategies of image registration and cell segmentation as in another work43 for identifying single cells in Stereo-seq data. Initially, we converted the captured mRNAs of each section into a 16-bit image, with the UMI counts of each coordinate as its pixel value. Next, nucleic acid staining images of sections were automatically registered into the corresponding mRNA coordinate spaces, utilizing the periodical track lines pre-engraved in the chip planes. In this step, we first applied adaptive brightness and contract adjustment on the images, enhancing the features and reducing the impact of uneven staining. We then employed 1D Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) operators, used separately in the row and column directions, to detect track lines in both nucleic acid staining and mRNA images and estimate the relative rotation between the two channels. The relative scale and translation were next calculated based on the detected periodical track lines using RANSAC algorithm. The image registration procedure was implemented with Scikit-image package (v.0.19.2) in Python (v.3.9.7).

This process was repeated until all 7 ConA images had their labels corrected. Subsequently, these corrected labels were transferred to their corresponding nucleic acid images for training the nucleic acid model. The ConA model was specifically utilized to aid in the generation of cell labels. After several iterations, a full set of cell annotations on ConA staining images were generated (14212 in the current experiment). The detailed information of the active learning procedure can be found in Table S4. After that, the cell annotations were transferred to the corresponding nucleic acid staining images to train another deep learning model on the nucleic acid staining images, called nucleic acid model. Noted that the nucleic acid model was trained with incomplete annotations since ConA images have fewer stained cells than nucleic acid images. Therefore, a low score threshold of 0.1 was applied to retain more cells. The nucleic acid model was deployed on nucleic acid staining images to obtain single cell segmentation. The nucleic acid model was validated on 10,209 cells from three nucleic acid staining images and achieved 0.912 of precision and 0.913 of recall, demonstrating reliable performance. All models described in this step were implemented with mmdet package (v.2.25.1) in Python (v.3.8.13).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] To segment single cells in nucleic acid staining images, we leveraged mask R-CNN-based deep learning models that were trained with annotations from Concanavalin A (ConA) staining images. ConA staining images, which stain the cell membranes, provide distinct boundaries between cells, hence facilitating easier distinction and manual annotation as compared to nucleic acid staining images. For the training set annotation, we used an active learning strategy, keeping human involvement to a minimum. To start, we manually labeled a small number of cells in the ConA images for training a mask R-CNN-based deep learning model, denoted as ConA model. The trained ConA model was applied to predict the cells of unlabeled ConA images. After a manual check and modification, these cell labels were then sent back to update the ConA model. We continued the cyclic process until enough annotations were acquired. The obtained cell annotations of ConA images were transferred to the corresponding nuclei acid staining images as the training set of another mask R-CNN-based deep learning model, denoted as nucleic acid model. Finally, the well-trained nuclei acid model was deployed on nucleic acid staining images to perform single cell segmentation. The cell segmentation procedure was implemented with MMDetection package (v.2.25.1) in Python (v.3.8.13).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Cells in nucleic acid staining images were automatically segmented through a deep learning model trained using annotations by ConA staining image. ConA staining images stain the membranes of cells, forming clear boundaries between cells, where cells are easier to be distinguished and manually marked than using nucleic acid staining images alone. However, ConA images have the problem of under-staining where not all cells would be clearly stained, and it is also tedious to manually mark every cell on the image. Therefore, we designed an active learning procedure. We first manually marked cells which could be clearly identified in ConA staining images. Starting with this small set (hundreds of cells), we trained a deep learning model (i.e. mask R-CNN78) on the ConA staining images, called ConA model. We utilized a total of 7 ConA images to construct the ConA model. One of these images was manually labeled and kept aside for validation purposes. The remaining 6 ConA images were employed for model training and underwent manual correction. The training process was conducted progressively as follows: Initially, we manually labeled the first image to train the initial ConA model. Subsequently, this trained ConA model was used to predict cell labels on the second unlabeled ConA image. After manual correction, the newly labeled ConA image was included in the training set to update the ConA model. This process was repeated until all 7 ConA images had their labels corrected.

Retrograde tracing procedures were performed as previously described. The CTB 647 and FastBlue tracer were used for tracer injection in the entorhinal cortex and primary motor cortex, respectively. Coronal sections of the claustrum were collected, and fluorescent images were collected for identification of labeled claustral projection neurons. Subsequently, Stereo-seq experiments and data processing were performed as described above.

For claustral-cortical projection strength (retrograde tracer injections in cortical areas), the FLN value was defined as the fraction of labeled claustral neurons relative to the total labeled cells across the entire brain (both hemispheres, including cortical areas and subcortical structures). The projection strength of ipsilateral and contralateral claustrum to a specific target area were calculated separately. For cortical and subcortical inputs to claustrum (retrograde tracer injections in the claustrum), we used the extrinsic fraction of labeled neurons (FLNe) to quantify the connection strength. For a specific cortical area or subcortical structure, the FLNe was calculated as the fraction of labeled cells in the specific region relative to the total cells labeled in the entire brain except claustrum. Higher FLN values indicate stronger connection.

Next, we performed Gaussian Kernel Density Estimation $( { \mathsf { K D E } } ) ^ { 8 0 }$ on each section to calculate the density estimation. Then, we populated a grid matrix with the estimated values at a resolution of 65 mm/pixel. We then extracted contours using a threshold of 0.05. If necessary, manual adjustments were made to eliminate obvious outlier. The regions defined by these extracted contours the on these 42 sections were defined as the distributions zone.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] snRNA-seq library construction and sequencing The DNBelab C Series High-throughput Single-cell System (BGI-research) was employed for the preparation of snRNA-seq libraries. In summary, the single-nucleus suspensions underwent several steps using this system, including droplet encapsulation, emulsion breakage, collection of mRNA-captured beads, reverse transcription, cDNA amplification, and purification to convert them into barcoded snRNA-seq libraries. The generated cDNA was fragmented into short segments of 250-400 bp, and indexed sequencing libraries were then constructed following the provided guidelines. Quality assessment was carried out utilizing the Qubit ssDNA Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100. Subsequently, all libraries underwent sequencing on the DIPSEQ T1 platform (China National GeneBank) using pair-end sequencing. The sequencing data comprised a 30-bp read 1 (comprising a 10-bp cell barcode 1, a 10-bp cell barcode 2, and 10-bp unique molecular identifiers (UMI)), a 100-bp read 2 for gene sequences, and a 10-bp barcode read for sample indexing.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Stereo-seq data processing Stereo-seq data processingThe fastq files of Stereo-seq were processed according to the previously described workflow.28 The first reads of the Stereo-seq data contained CID (coordinate Identity) sequences, which were aligned to the designed coordinates of the Stereo-seq chip obtained from the first round of sequencing. A maximum of 1 base mismatch was allowed during the alignment process. Reads with MID (molecular Identifiers) containing N bases or more than 2 bases with quality score lower than 10 were removed from the dataset. The CID and MID associated with each read were added to the read header. The retained reads were then aligned to the reference genome using STAR74 and reads with mapping quality score $> 1 0$ were counted and annotated to their corresponding genes. UMIs that have the same CID (coordinate Identity) and gene locus were combined into a single UMI, allowing for 1 mismatch to correct for sequencing and PCR errors. Finally, this information was used to generate a CID-containing expression profile matrix. The entire pipeline SAW can be accessed at https://github.com/STOmics/SAW.

question: What were the eight major cell types identified from the unsupervised clustering of snRNA-seq data?
retrieved_docs: [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Cell clustering and cell type identification using snRNA-seq data Cell clustering and annotation of snRNA-seq data were conducted using Seurat (v4.1.1) in R (v4.1.3). In previous step, nuclei were categorized into 8 class based on their marker genes: excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, $D R D 2 +$ inhibitory neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells, microglia and endothelial cells, while doublets and low-quality cells were removed. Subsequently, we iteratively classified the seven classes into more refined, higher-resolution cell clusters.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] After quality control (STAR Methods), the snRNA-seq analysis included 227,750 cells, with an average of 4,664 molecular identifiers (MIDs) per cell and 1,884 detected genes per cell (Figure S1A). Our UMAP analysis identified three major cell classes (‘‘glutamatergic’’ [GLUT]: 122,006 cells; ‘‘GABAergic’’ [GABA]: 34,293 cells; ‘‘non-neuronal’’: 71,451 cells), which were further divided into 16 subclasses (Figure 1B), including 3 glutamatergic (marked by GNB4, RGS6, and ZFPM2), 8 GABAergic (LAMP5, VIP, RELN, PVALB, SST, PDE10A, LHX6, and UNC5B), and 5 non-neuronal subclasses, including astrocytes (SLC1A2), oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs, PCDH15), oligodendrocytes (MOBP), microglia (C1QB), and endothelial cells (FLT1). Most subclasses contained cells from all four monkeys (Figure S1B), confirming data reproducibility, which was further validated by random forest analysis (Figure S1C). The 16 subclasses could be further divided into 48 putative ‘‘cell types’’: 22 glutamatergic, 19 GABAergic, and 7 non-neuronal cell types (Figures 1C and S1D; Table S1). retrieved_docs: [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Registration of claustrum boundaries on coronal sections across different animals We registered the claustra of all animals to one with high-quality sections. The method we used was a convolutional Siamese neural network that computed a 16-dimensional embedding of the claustrum. ResNet18 was used as the feature extraction backbone, with cosine distance as the loss function. Dropout was added after the backbone to improve abstraction capability. During training, we used dropout $= 0 . 2 5$ , AdamW optimizer with hyperparameters $\mathsf { l } \mathsf { r } = \mathsf { \Omega } \mathsf { l } \mathsf { e } ^ { - 3 }$ , $\beta \mathbf { 5 } = ( 0 . 9 , \ 0 . 9 9 9 )$ , $\lambda = 1 { \mathsf e } ^ { - 2 }$ , and data augmentation including random rotation $( \boldsymbol { 0 } = \pm 4 5 ^ { \circ } )$ ), random left-right flip $( \mathsf { p } = 0 . 5 )$ ), random translation $( \pm 2 0 \%$ on x, $\pm 1 0 \%$ on y), and random scaling $( 0 . 9 \sim 1 . 1 \times )$ . These augmentations were inspired by the deviations that occur when mounting the tissue sections onto the slides. We trained for 2000 epochs in total.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Claustrum segmentation from coronal sections We trained a model using nnUNet79 to segment the claustrum from coronal sections. The hyperparameters were set to the default values of nnUNet. The supervised data came from manually plotted claustrum boundaries by human experts. The input images were acquired from a fluorescence microscope with four scanning channels: Cy3 (582 - 640 nm), Cy5 (670 - 710 nm), EGFP (507 - 543 nm), and DAPI (430 - 470 nm). The original resolution of the images was 0.65 mm/pixel. To reduce computational cost, we down-sampled the images at a resolution of 13 mm/pixel. We then trained the model with 20 manually segmented claustrum (evenly spaced at $6 2 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } } )$ ) sections from one monkey. After training, we used the model to segment the claustrum in the remaining sections, which were then inspected and corrected by experts for any inconsistencies. We retrained the model using the full set of corrected slices, and used the model to segment the claustrum for other animals. For animals with notably inconsistent results, human experts provided additional corrections. By iteratively processing all animals as described above, we segmented the claustrum from all coronal slices, which passed the inspection of human experts. The software and versions involved in this process were: nnUNet (v.2.2), Python (v.3.11.3), PyTorch (v.2.0.1), and CellPlot (v.1.005).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Determination of the distribution zone (DZ) of claustral projecting neurons and clustering analysis of DZs For each tracer injection at a particular brain area, we determined the distribution zone of retrograde dye-labeled claustral neurons as follows: First, we outlined the claustrum in 42 ipsilateral coronal sections for each animal, with a spacing of $3 6 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ . The regions defined by these extracted contours the on these 42 sections were defined as the distributions zone.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Quantification of spatial distribution of various cell types in the Stereo-seq map Given the significant variation in shape among different individuals and coronal sections of the claustrum, we employed a standardization technique to establish relative dorsal-ventral and medial-lateral positions. Specifically, the normalized layer and column values were calculated by solving a partial differential equation known as the heat equation within the defined claustrum area. To define the boundary conditions of the claustrum, four user-provided coordinates were utilized to determine the direction of the gradient. The resulting values from the digitalization process were used to establish standardized spatial grids across the various coronal sections and individuals. The digitalization procedure was implemented with spateo package (v.1.0.2) (https://github. com/aristoteleo/spateo-release) in Python (v.3.9.16).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Image registration and image-based single cell segmentation of Stereo-seq data We performed the same strategies of image registration and cell segmentation as in another work43 for identifying single cells in Stereo-seq data. Initially, we converted the captured mRNAs of each section into a 16-bit image, with the UMI counts of each coordinate as its pixel value. Next, nucleic acid staining images of sections were automatically registered into the corresponding mRNA coordinate spaces, utilizing the periodical track lines pre-engraved in the chip planes. In this step, we first applied adaptive brightness and contract adjustment on the images, enhancing the features and reducing the impact of uneven staining. We then employed 1D Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) operators, used separately in the row and column directions, to detect track lines in both nucleic acid staining and mRNA images and estimate the relative rotation between the two channels. The relative scale and translation were next calculated based on the detected periodical track lines using RANSAC algorithm. The image registration procedure was implemented with Scikit-image package (v.0.19.2) in Python (v.3.9.7).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] MRI scanning Premedication and induced anesthesia were performed by the same procedure as that described for retrograde tracer injection experiments. During MRI scanning, $1 . 0 \% - 1 . 5 \%$ isoflurane in pure oxygen were used to maintain anesthesia. MRI scanning was carried out with 8 channel coil (SuZhouZhongZhi, MK80-3T) and 3.0T MRI scanner (Siemens). Magnetization prepared rapid gradient echo image (MPRAGE) sequence $( 0 . 5 \mathsf { m m }$ isotropic resolution, T $\equiv = 2 . 8 \mathsf { m s }$ , ${ \mathsf { T R } } = 2 2 0 0 { \mathsf { m s } }$ , $\mathsf E \mathsf A = 9$ degree, number of average $= 4$ ) was used to obtain T1w structural images.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Cell clustering and cell-type identification using snRNA-seq data Cell clustering and cell-type identification using snRNA-seq dataBasic processing and visualization of the snRNA-seq data were performed with the Scanpy (v.1.9.1) in Python (v.3.8.13). We discarded cells with the number of genes (nFeatureRNA) less than 1000, the molecule to gene ratio (nCount/nFeature) less than 1.2 and the percentage of mitochondrial genes (percent.mt) larger than $5 \%$ . After the first quality control, 1,493,240 cells were remained for the following analyses. The data were log normalized and scaled to 10,000 transcripts per cell. Genes with high variations across cells were identified with the ‘‘sc.pp.highly_variable_genes’’ function with default parameters (top 3000). Next, principal component analysis (PCA) was carried out, and the top 40 principal components (PCs) were used by BBKNN method to remove the batch effect among two macaques. Graph-based clustering (Leiden) was performed with resolution of 1.0 on the graph-representation output of BBKNN. This method resulted in 33 cell clusters. We used uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) method to visualize the distance between cells in 2D space. We then categorized the 33 cell clusters into 3 categories based on classical marker genes, including glutamatergic neurons, GABAergic neurons and non-neuronal cells. Then the three categories of cells were further iteratively classified into more cell clusters with higher resolution.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Image registration and image-based single cell segmentation of Stereo-seq data We performed the same strategies of image registration and cell segmentation as in another work43 for identifying single cells in Stereo-seq data. Initially, we converted the captured mRNAs of each section into a 16-bit image, with the UMI counts of each coordinate as its pixel value. Next, nucleic acid staining images of sections were automatically registered into the corresponding mRNA coordinate spaces, utilizing the periodical track lines pre-engraved in the chip planes. In this step, we first applied adaptive brightness and contract adjustment on the images, enhancing the features and reducing the impact of uneven staining. We then employed 1D Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) operators, used separately in the row and column directions, to detect track lines in both nucleic acid staining and mRNA images and estimate the relative rotation between the two channels. The relative scale and translation were next calculated based on the detected periodical track lines using RANSAC algorithm. The image registration procedure was implemented with Scikit-image package (v.0.19.2) in Python (v.3.9.7).

Based on their gene expression profiles and localization in the stereo-seq map (see section below), glutamatergic neuron subclasses were annotated by their layer preferences (L for layer: L2, L2/3, L2/3/4, L3/4, L3/4/5, L4, L4/5, L4/5/6, L5/6, and L6; see STAR Methods). GABAergic neuron subclasses were annotated by 5 prominent marker genes: lysosome-associated membrane protein 5 (LAMP5), vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), reelin (RELN), parvalbumin (PV), and somatostatin (SST).12,15,16 We noted that the interneuron marker gene calbindin (CALB1) is mainly expressed by SST and LAMP5 subclasses, and the calretinin gene (CALB2) is mainly expressed by VIP and VIP_RELN subclasses (Figure S1K). [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Notably, our study revealed several rules of cellular organization with respect to cortical hierarchy. First, all three major cell classes contain cell types with their regional densities positively or negatively correlated with the cortical hierarchy of the visual and somatosensory systems. Second, many cell types showing positive or negative correlation with hierarchy are shared by these sensory systems. Third, the number of glutamatergic cell types with negative correlation with hierarchy is much higher than that of GABAergic cell types. Finally, the regional distribution of non-neuronal cell types only exhibits positive correlations with the hierarchy level. These organization rules on cell-type distribution may underlie the increasing complexity of information processing with the hierarchy level and provide the basis for further studying the specific roles of various cell types in cortical functions at different hierarchy levels. Furthermore, the increased expression of the glutamatergic receptor genes and the decreasing density of various glutamatergic cell types along the hierarchy level imply that the expression of these genes is increasingly elevated in each cell with its hierarchy level, consistent with the elevated spine density in neurons.68

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] SUMMARY Claustrum orchestrates brain functions via its connections with numerous brain regions, but its molecular and cellular organization remains unresolved. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 227,750 macaque claustral cells identified 48 transcriptome-defined cell types, with most glutamatergic neurons similar to deep-layer insular neurons. Comparison of macaque, marmoset,and mouse transcriptomes revealed macaque-specific cell types. Retrograde tracer injections at 67 cortical and 7 subcortical regions defined four distinct distribution zones of retrogradely labeled claustral neurons. Joint analysis of whole-brain connectivity and single-cell spatial transcriptome showed that these four zones containing distinct compositions of glutamatergic (but not GABAergic) cell types preferentially connected to specific brain regions with a strong ipsilateral bias. Several macaque-specific glutamatergic cell types in ventral vs. dorsal claustral zones selectively co-projected to two functionally related areas—entorhinal cortex and hippocampus vs. motor cortex and putamen, respectively. These data provide the basis for elucidating the neuronal organization underlying diverse claustral functions.

We first determined the region in the spatial transcriptome map (Figure 6A; STAR Methods) that corresponded to the DZ of claustral projection neurons defined by tracer injection at each of the 156 cortical (Figure 4A), 9 subcortical, and 5 intra-claustrum sites. The density of various claustral glutamatergic cell types within each DZ was calculated, and the normalized density of each cell type across all DZs was then determined. question: How many clusters were identified in the marmoset and macaque claustrum snRNA-seq data?
retrieved_docs: [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Cross-species integration of claustrum snRNA-seq cells Claustrum tissue samples from mouse and marmosets were collected and conducted single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq). The obtained single-nucleus sequencing libraries underwent identical data preprocessing steps as those performed on the macaque samples. Subsequently, we identified 234,986 cells from the mouse claustrum and 109,093 cells from the marmoset claustrum. Clustering and annotation of the single-nucleus sequencing data from mouse and marmosets followed the same procedures as described in above section, utilizing the same marker genes as those used for the macaque claustrum. Specifically, marmoset data were partitioned into 38 clusters, whereas mouse data were divided into 60 clusters. Moreover, using high variable genes identified from the macaque subclass, we annotated subclasses in mice and marmosets, resulting in 16 subclasses for each species.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] Cell type transcriptomics within GNB4 subclasses were further compared across the three species by integrating analysis. To ensure consistency in cell numbers across regions, for each macaque cluster, 1,200 cells were selected, with all available cells used if the cluster contained fewer than 1,200. Similarly, 1,500 cells were selected per marmoset cluster and 6,000 per mouse cluster, using all available cells if the cluster sizes were smaller than these thresholds. After down-sampling, this resulted in approximately 13,200 macaque cells, 11,706 marmoset cells, and 12,506 mouse cells. We then merged the datasets of the three species based on homologous genes, which were obtained from the Ensembl (https://useast.ensembl.org/index.html). The merged dataset was normalized using ‘Seurat::NormalizeData‘ and then subjected to dimensionality reduction with ‘Seurat::RunPCA‘. We employed the modified ‘RunHarmony‘ function in the Harmony package (v0.1.0) to integrate data across species. The cell type overlap score across different species was calculated using the Release q1wPipeline script (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34616062/). For each pair of macaque and mouse clusters, the overlap was defined as the proportion of clusters in the macaque that co-cluster with clusters in the marmoset or mouse. The co-clustering proportion was calculated by determining the minimum value for each pair of clusters and then summing these minimum values. Cluster overlaps varied from 0 to 1, and were visualized as a heat map with macaque clusters in rows and mouse clusters in columns.

We applied wilcoxon rank sum test using the ‘‘sc.tl.rangk_genes_groups’’ function for differential gene expression analysis among clusters. Genes with ${ \mathsf { l o g } } _ { 2 }$ fold-change $> 1$ and $\mathsf { F D R } < 0 . 0 5$ were retained as significant marker genes for the cluster. The top 50 DEG were selected as features, and 100 cells were randomly sampled from each cluster, of which $80 \%$ of the cells were used to train the model, and the rest $20 \%$ as a validation dataset. retrieved_docs: [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] SUMMARY Elucidating the cellular organization of the cerebral cortex is critical for understanding brain structure and function. Using large-scale single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic analysis of 143 macaque cortical regions, we obtained a comprehensive atlas of 264 transcriptome-defined cortical cell types and mapped their spatial distribution across the entire cortex. We characterized the cortical layer and region preferences of glutamatergic, GABAergic, and non-neuronal cell types, as well as regional differences in celltype composition and neighborhood complexity. Notably, we discovered a relationship between the regional distribution of various cell types and the region’s hierarchical level in the visual and somatosensory systems. Cross-species comparison of transcriptomic data from human, macaque, and mouse cortices further revealed primate-specific cell types that are enriched in layer 4, with their marker genes expressed in a region-dependent manner. Our data provide a cellular and molecular basis for understanding the evolution, development, aging, and pathogenesis of the primate brain.

In combination with a large-scale single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) analysis, we obtained a comprehensive 3D single-cell atlas for the cortex of cynomolgus monkey. This enabled a systematic analysis of the cortical-layer- and region-specific distributions of cell types and their molecular fingerprints and discovery of the relationship between cell-type composition and hierarchical organization of the visual and somatosensory systems. [source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Notably, our study revealed several rules of cellular organization with respect to cortical hierarchy. First, all three major cell classes contain cell types with their regional densities positively or negatively correlated with the cortical hierarchy of the visual and somatosensory systems. Second, many cell types showing positive or negative correlation with hierarchy are shared by these sensory systems. Third, the number of glutamatergic cell types with negative correlation with hierarchy is much higher than that of GABAergic cell types. Finally, the regional distribution of non-neuronal cell types only exhibits positive correlations with the hierarchy level. These organization rules on cell-type distribution may underlie the increasing complexity of information processing with the hierarchy level and provide the basis for further studying the specific roles of various cell types in cortical functions at different hierarchy levels. Furthermore, the increased expression of the glutamatergic receptor genes and the decreasing density of various glutamatergic cell types along the hierarchy level imply that the expression of these genes is increasingly elevated in each cell with its hierarchy level, consistent with the elevated spine density in neurons.68

The sequencing data within the manually annotated cortex region were processed with the Seurat package in R. The cell-by-gene matrix was obtained with the function ‘‘CreateSeuratObject’’ with min.cells $= 3$ and min.features $= 0$ . The percentage of mitochondrial genes (percent.mt) was calculated with the function ‘‘PercentageFeatureSet’’ (using genes ND6, COX3, COX1, ND5, ND4, ND2, ND4L, ATP8, CYTB, COX2, ND3, ATP6 and ND1). Cells with less than 100 features or percent.mt larger than $1 5 \%$ were discarded. In order to mitigate potential batch effects resulting from variations in single-cell sequencing depth within and across sections of the Stereo-seq map, ‘‘SCTransform’’ with the parameter vars.to.regress $=$ ‘‘percent.mt’’ was used for normalization.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Each stereo-seq section was stained with a dye specific to nucleic acid28 and a fluorescence-labeled lectin, concanavalin A (ConA), that marks the plasma membrane (Figures 2A and S2A). An artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted automatic segmentation method was developed for single-cell identification based on nucleic acid and ConA images (see STAR Methods and Table S4). The reliability of automatic identification was shown by high recall and precision rates (Figures 2B and S2B). Using this method, we obtained 266,310 segmented cortical cells per section with an average of 819 unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) and 458 genes per cell (Figure 2C; Table S3). The average number of genes per cell was much higher than that in background $1 . 5 \pm 0 . 9$ genes/bin) and that in $1 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } } \times 1 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ bins (each containing $2 0 \times 2 0$ DNBs; $1 4 7 \pm 8 2$ genes/bin) across entire sections (Figure 2C).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Stereo-seq data processing Stereo-seq data processingThe fastq files of Stereo-seq were processed according to the previously described workflow.28 The first reads of the Stereo-seq data contained CID (coordinate Identity) sequences, which were aligned to the designed coordinates of the Stereo-seq chip obtained from the first round of sequencing. A maximum of 1 base mismatch was allowed during the alignment process. Reads with MID (molecular Identifiers) containing N bases or more than 2 bases with quality score lower than 10 were removed from the dataset. The CID and MID associated with each read were added to the read header. The retained reads were then aligned to the reference genome using STAR74 and reads with mapping quality score $> 1 0$ were counted and annotated to their corresponding genes. UMIs that have the same CID (coordinate Identity) and gene locus were combined into a single UMI, allowing for 1 mismatch to correct for sequencing and PCR errors. Finally, this information was used to generate a CID-containing expression profile matrix. The entire pipeline SAW can be accessed at https://github.com/STOmics/SAW.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_atlas_and_whole-brain_connectivity_of_the_macaque_claustrum.md] After quality control (STAR Methods), the snRNA-seq analysis included 227,750 cells, with an average of 4,664 molecular identifiers (MIDs) per cell and 1,884 detected genes per cell (Figure S1A). Our UMAP analysis identified three major cell classes (‘‘glutamatergic’’ [GLUT]: 122,006 cells; ‘‘GABAergic’’ [GABA]: 34,293 cells; ‘‘non-neuronal’’: 71,451 cells), which were further divided into 16 subclasses (Figure 1B), including 3 glutamatergic (marked by GNB4, RGS6, and ZFPM2), 8 GABAergic (LAMP5, VIP, RELN, PVALB, SST, PDE10A, LHX6, and UNC5B), and 5 non-neuronal subclasses, including astrocytes (SLC1A2), oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs, PCDH15), oligodendrocytes (MOBP), microglia (C1QB), and endothelial cells (FLT1). Most subclasses contained cells from all four monkeys (Figure S1B), confirming data reproducibility, which was further validated by random forest analysis (Figure S1C). The 16 subclasses could be further divided into 48 putative ‘‘cell types’’: 22 glutamatergic, 19 GABAergic, and 7 non-neuronal cell types (Figures 1C and S1D; Table S1). Using ‘‘spatial-ID,’’39 we annotated cells in Stereo-seq maps from two macaques, matching them to the 48 snRNA-seq-defined cell types (STAR Methods). The cell-type distribution was consistent across monkeys (Figure S1E), with the proportions of various cell types similar to those found by snRNA-seq analysis (Figure S1F).

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Tissue-section processing for stereo-seq Tissue-section processing for stereo-seqThe tissue section on the Stereo-seq chip (5 cm x 3 cm or 2 cm x 3 cm) was then incubated at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 5-8 min and subsequently fixed in methanol (Sigma, 34860, precooled for 30 mins at $\scriptstyle - 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ ; 40 ml methanol was added in $1 0 \mathsf { c m }$ dish for each section) and incubated at $\scriptstyle - 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ for 30 minutes. Methanol was then dried out in a hood. Tissue section on the chip was then stained with mixture of nucleic acid reagent (Invitrogen, Q10212) and conA Rhodamine (Vector, RL-1002, working concentration $2 0 0 ~ { \mu \ g / \ m \up| }$ ) for 5 min and subsequently washed with 0.1x SSC buffer (Ambion, AM9770; containing $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { { U } / \mu \mu \mu }$ RNase inhibitor). Section images were captured using Zeiss Axio Scan Z1 microscope (at EGFP wavelength, 10-ms exposure). Tissue sections were then permeated by incubating in $0 . 1 \%$ pepsin (Sigma, P7000) at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 15 minutes (pepsin was prewarmed at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 3 min) in 0.01M HCl buffer (pH 2) and then washed with 0.1xSSC buffer (containing $0 . 0 5 \ : \mathrm { U / \mu l }$ RNase inhibitor) to remove pepsin. In this step, RNAs were released from the permeated tissue and captured by Stereo-seq chip. RNAs were then reverse transcribed for 2 hours at $4 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ .

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Spatial distribution of diverse cell types across the macaque cortex We used stereo-seq to capture mRNAs from all cells of each brain section in close contact with a large silicon chip (up to $5 \mathsf { c m } \times 3 \mathsf { c m }$ ), which comprised regular 2D arrays of DNA nanoballs (DNBs; size, 220 nm; center to center, $5 0 0 \mathsf { n m }$ ). We developed a section-flattening method after cryo-sectioning to obtain even and smooth surface contact between large brain sections and stereo-seq chips (see STAR Methods). Stereo-seq analysis was performed on $1 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ coronal sections from the freshly isolated left hemisphere of three adult male cynomolgus monkeys. In monkey #1, we obtained a total of 119 sections at $5 0 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ spacing covering the entire cortex (Table S3), together with two 10- $\mu \mathsf { m }$ sections adjacent to each stereo-seq section for immunostaining and several adjacent $5 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ thick sections for regional microdissection and snRNA-seq analysis (see above, Figure 1A). For biological replication, we also obtained $1 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ sections from two other monkeys (19 sections from #2 and 23 sections from #3, 3-mm spacing; Table S3). The $1 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ section thickness, together with section preservation procedures that reduced mRNA diffusion, facilitated spatial transcriptome analysis at the single-cell resolution.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Quantification of spatial distribution of various cell types in the stereo-seq map Quantification of spatial distribution of various cell types in the stereo-seq mapWe quantified the number of cells annotated with specific cell types in each monkey and cell types with more than 1000 cells in the three monkeys were used for the following analysis. For each cell type, we quantified the density in each layer and cortical region by dividing the total number of cells in each area by the area size. To quantify the layer distribution of various glutamatergic neuron types, we performed z-score transformation of cell density in each cortical layer for each cell type, and layers with z-score larger than 0 were used to annotate the subclass name of each glutamatergic cell type together with marker gene expression.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] We further constructed a three-level taxonomy tree using the hierarchical clustering of these cell types (Figure 1B; Table S2). Level 1 represents three major cell classes: glutamatergic (969,794), GABAergic (268,097) and non-neuronal (97,298) cells. Level 2 comprised subclasses of these three major classes, each with distinct subclass marker genes (Figures 1B, S1J, and S1K). Based on their gene expression profiles and localization in the stereo-seq map (see section below), glutamatergic neuron subclasses were annotated by their layer preferences (L for layer: L2, L2/3, L2/3/4, L3/4, L3/4/5, L4, L4/5, L4/5/6, L5/6, and L6; see STAR Methods). The glutamatergic neuron subclasses showed substantial correspondence with the projection-property-inferred subclasses identified by the Allen Institute16 (Figure S1L). GABAergic neuron subclasses were annotated by 5 prominent marker genes: lysosome-associated membrane protein 5 (LAMP5), vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), reelin (RELN), parvalbumin (PV), and somatostatin (SST).12,15,16 We noted that the interneuron marker gene calbindin (CALB1) is mainly expressed by SST and LAMP5 subclasses, and the calretinin gene (CALB2) is mainly expressed by VIP and VIP_RELN subclasses (Figure S1K). The 6 non-neuronal subclasses included astrocytes (ASCs), oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), oligodendrocytes (OLGs), microglia (MG), endothelial cells (ECs), and vascular leptomeningeal cells (VLMCs), each annotated by their specific marker genes (Figure S1K).

Level 3 represents further classification of subclasses, including 264 cell clusters (termed hereafter ‘‘types’’). Each level 3 cell type was annotated by level 1 and 2 labels and two top-rank differentially expressed genes (DEGs, Table S2). For example, the third type of glutamatergic cells found in L2 that highly expressed ART3/GPC5 was annotated as Glu L2.3-ART3/GPC5. For the sake of brevity, the cell-type name was simply referred to without marker genes in the figures, e.g., Glu L2.3-ART3/GPC5 as L2.3. This snRNAseq analysis incorporating spatial transcriptome information yielded a comprehensive cell-type taxonomy of the macaque cerebral cortex.

[source: Single-cell_spatial_transcriptome_revealscell-type_organization_in_the_macaque_cortex.md] Notably, our study revealed several rules of cellular organization with respect to cortical hierarchy. First, all three major cell classes contain cell types with their regional densities positively or negatively correlated with the cortical hierarchy of the visual and somatosensory systems. Second, many cell types showing positive or negative correlation with hierarchy are shared by these sensory systems. Third, the number of glutamatergic cell types with negative correlation with hierarchy is much higher than that of GABAergic cell types. Finally, the regional distribution of non-neuronal cell types only exhibits positive correlations with the hierarchy level. These organization rules on cell-type distribution may underlie the increasing complexity of information processing with the hierarchy level and provide the basis for further studying the specific roles of various cell types in cortical functions at different hierarchy levels. Furthermore, the increased expression of the glutamatergic receptor genes and the decreasing density of various glutamatergic cell types along the hierarchy level imply that the expression of these genes is increasingly elevated in each cell with its hierarchy level, consistent with the elevated spine density in neurons.68
